title: London tourist tax on accommodation will be capped at 5pc, mayor says
text:
A new tax on overnight stays in London will be capped at 5 per cent of the cost of accommodation, the BBC has reported.

Under the legislation, local authorities will be able to charge a flat fee or a percentage of the cost of an overnight stay for domestic and international guests in London accommodations.

London Mayor Sir Sadiq Khan told BBC London that he welcomed plans by the government and promised it would not be above 5 per cent per night.

The exact amount has not yet been determined.

"I fully support the government's decision, after years of lobbying, to give us the same powers that other cities, from New York to Los Angeles, from Chicago to Paris … have, which is the ability to raise a levy on those who come to our great city," he said.

"We've got to invest in making sure that [our] city continues to be attractive."

There are concerns the costs could put visitors off heading to London, an extremely popular destination for Australians heading abroad.

How will the tax work?

Between November of last year and February of 2026, the UK government consulted on the design of a new power for English councils to introduce overnight visitor levies or a "tourist tax".

London 'tourist tax' proposed for international travellers Australians heading to England could soon pay a new "tourist tax" on accommodation.

The legal framework to do so will be introduced in the Overnight Visitor Levy bill, which has not yet been tabled in parliament.

A visitor levy set by English mayors would apply to hotels, guesthouses, bed and breakfasts, hostels, campsites, self-catering properties, and short-term lets, and university and religious accommodation when let commercially.

The levy would be set as a percentage of the price of the accommodation.

Mayors would be able to set local exemptions.

They would also be able to choose to set a visitor levy in some of their local authority areas but not others.

Members of the combined authority would be able to reject a levy by a two-thirds majority.

It will bring England in line with Scotland and Wales, which have already introduced powers for local authorities to raise a visitor levy.

Why is it being implemented?

The bill proposes that English mayors can spend revenue from the levy for "broader initiatives which have a positive impact on the region's economic health."

"Mayors will be empowered to deliver more long-term, locally led investment in transport, regeneration and cultural assets that can unlock growth and make places more attractive for residents, businesses and visitors," the bill said.

"The government will not compel any mayor to introduce this levy, nor will central government reduce funding for mayors if they decide to do so."

The levy could raise up to £240 million ($450 million) annually, according to Central London Forward, which represents 12 London local authorities and is based on a 3 per cent levy on the cost of a room.

Where else has it been applied?

Similar schemes have been implemented around the world.

In Europe, a city tax is the norm for many popular locations, including Venice, Rome, Amsterdam, Barcelona and Berlin and is used to fund local infrastructure and manage over-tourism.

In Paris, travellers pay from $2 to $15 per night depending on how the hotel is rated.

In New York, several taxes are applied to an overnight stay, which total about 14 per cent per night.

Japan also charges an overnight stay tax for foreign visitors per night.

How has Australia responded?

According to the most recent data from Visit Britain, 1.2 million Australians travelled to the UK in 2024.

During the travellers' visits, their total expenditure was a record £1.7 billion, with an average spend of £1,358 ($2,561) per visit.

Australians have criticised the proposed changes amid the growing expenses of overseas travel.

Australian Travel Industry Association chief executive Dean Long previously told the ABC the decision to tax travellers would add to an already expensive long-haul destination at the top of many Aussies' bucket lists.

"We're entering a new era where governments are increasingly targeting travellers with taxes," he said.

"It's a never-ending battle that ultimately means less money spent in the economy and less revenue for the small businesses employing the people who deliver the experiences."

title: Zak Butters fixes sights on Western Bulldogs move
text:
Port Adelaide midfielder Zak Butters has nominated Western Bulldogs as his preferred club, weeks after announcing his decision to head home to Victoria.

In a statement on Saturday morning, the Western Bulldogs confirmed Butters had informed the club of his desire to join.



"The club will work with Port Adelaide to facilitate a suitable outcome during the upcoming player movement period," the Bulldogs said.

The 26-year-old's future had dominated headlines during the season with reports of offers over eight years from Richmond, Geelong, Collingwood and the Western Bulldogs.

Butters had narrowed his choice to the Bulldogs and Geelong before settling on the club he supported as a child.

He has reportedly been offered a nine-year deal worth up to $2 million per season to join Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards in a high-powered Dogs engine room.

But Port Adelaide has the right to match the bid for restricted free agent Butters and force the Bulldogs into a trade for the three-time All-Australian.

On August 24, Butters announced his decision to "head home", saying it was a "tough decision and one that I haven't taken lightly".

"Although I've loved my time in Adelaide … I'm probably at a stage in my life where I'd like to get back around some family and friends and enjoy some more time with them," he said at the time.

Three-time All-Australian Butters won three best-and-fairest awards with Port and stood in as captain this year with regular skipper Connor Rozee sidelined by a serious hamstring injury.

Butters' last game in Power colours was a defeat to St Kilda in round 18, when he suffered an ankle syndesmosis injury that ended his season early.

Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge has long been an admirer of Butters and irked Port counterpart Josh Carr this season when openly addressing his club's desire to lure the star midfielder.

"Marcus [Bontempelli], and some of Marcus's teammates, are quite naturally drawn to Zak," Beveridge said in June.

"They played in the state team together [in February], so he's developed some relationships with some of the other boys who played in that game."

ABC / AAP

title: These girls fear new child protection laws will lead to 'lost generations'
text:
Surrounded by the ocean, where eucalypt forest stretches from the sand to meet the sky, the Tiwi Islands are a living library for the young people who call it home.

Etched into the landscape are guides on how to live off the land and language that describes their way of life, all of which has taught kids their traditional customs over generations.

The island and its community hold the knowledge that tells the story of each family and how they're connected.

But there are fears these connections to kin and culture are under threat.

Tahni and Shanina fear changes to NT laws could result in more young people losing vital kinship connections. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

These fears are acutely felt by 17-year-old Tiwi Island girls Shanina Kantilla and Tahni Thompson, who are cousins on their mother's side.

Even when they're hundreds of kilometres from home, the islands are never far from their minds.

Shanina recalls a happy childhood spent camping, hunting, swimming and fishing.

"It's very important, especially starting from a young age, learning about our culture, skin groups and also our country … where we inherit our tribes, the sacred sites, ceremony," she said.

Tahni also feels a deep connection to being Tiwi, having returned after spending part of her childhood in Darwin.

"It's like my safe place. Whenever I go to other places, I always feel homesick," she said.

Life on the Tiwi Islands

Hundreds of fans gathered for the 2026 senior men's grand final clash on the islands. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

The Tiwi Islands is known for many things — vibrant artwork, secluded fishing spots and die-hard footy fans — with some of Australia's most renowned AFL players coming out of the region.

"We have a local league of AFL and it gets really hectic around those times," Tahni said.

Melville Island's Imalu Tigers took home the premiership this year. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Tiwi culture is also embedded in the girls' schooling, with weekly lessons on country.

But the real tutoring starts young and comes from within families — grandparents, parents, aunties and uncles.

Shanina's mother and grandmother taught her cultural practices from a young age. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Shanina's pride in her family traditions shines through as she explains how she's been taught to take wood from the local paper bark trees to weave into baskets.

"We scrape all the wood out and when we're done, we have to boil it and then we fold it, and let it sit for about two, three hours," she said.

"Once it dries up, we come back and start doing our traditional paintings."

Shanina describes weaving baskets using wood collected from the paper bark trees. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Both girls are well aware past government policies prevented this cultural knowledge from being passed down.

"Since the missionaries came, they just changed everything," Tahni said.

"Some of the kids on the other island, [due to] the [Stolen] Generations, don't really speak Tiwi."

From the early 1900s, Catholic missions on the Tiwi Islands controlled much of daily life, influencing where people lived, who they married and the upbringing of their children.

For many families, the policies disrupted the transmission of language, cultural practices and traditional knowledge.

Today, cultural disconnection can take different forms.

Tahni has fond memories of growing up on the islands and learning from her elders. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Tahni knows this firsthand. Growing up away from her homelands, she felt as though a part of her identity was missing until she returned to the Tiwi Islands.

"I wouldn't want to be taken away from my family," she said.

"I would want to stay with them forever."

Deflating the 'political football'

People gather for Garma each year from across the nation and the world. (ABC News: Erin Byrne)

On the other side of the territory's coastline, as thousands gathered for the Garma festival, First Nations people voiced fears of a renewed threat to kinship systems and culture.

Culture is celebrated as children show off their skills at the nightly Bunggul (dance). (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

For almost 30 years, Yolŋu people have opened their ceremonial grounds to visitors. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Political leaders have been urged to engage with the young people most affected by their policies. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Just weeks before, the Northern Territory government announced changes to child protection laws which critics said weakened the Aboriginal Child Placement Principle.

National Indigenous children's commissioner Sue-Anne Hunter was among those fearing it would lead to more children removed from their communities.

"I'm not here in a battle, I'm here to protect our children and make sure they're safe," she said.

"I feel like it's a bit of political football for everybody, and that's not what our kids should be."

The child placement principle aims to keep Aboriginal children connected to family, community and culture when they enter care.

It prioritises placing children with family in the first instance, then the child's own First Nations community and then other First Nations carers.

Sue-Anne Hunter has spent just over a year in the role. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

But under the NT changes, introduced after the death of Kumanjayi Little Baby, the government no longer needs to try to place a child with their community or a First Nations carer if they can't be placed with family.

Sue-Anne Hunter sees devastating echoes of the past.

"No-one is saying that our children need to be unsafe. If a child needs to be removed, then that's the fact. The thing is that culture is part of safety. It's their identity," she said.

"Maybe they [the NT government] need to have a discussion with some Stolen Generation people about how being disconnected affected their lives."

Legal experts say the CLP has taken an increasingly punitive approach to youth crime. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Ms Hunter spent much of her time at Garma hearing directly from young people, many of whom told her they were anxious about the changes.

"It's front of mind for youth as well," she said.

"We need to be investing in the front end. Family support, getting into families early, not waiting until we're ready to remove them."

Hundreds of young people attend Garma and take part in the youth forum. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

A spokesperson for the NT government denied the changes were weakening protections for Aboriginal children.

"These reforms — designed after extensive consultation — created a Universal Child Placement Principle so the same strong provisions apply to every child," they said.

"Additional provisions have been retained for Aboriginal children that reflect their cultural needs and connection to family, community and country."

Child protection isn't the only policy change adding to Ms Hunter's workload.

Sue-Anne Hunter told attendees she would "tell you the truth about how this nation is treating your children". (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

In recent years the NT lowered the age of criminal responsibility and reintroduced spit hoods, the NT, Victoria and Queensland removed the principle of detention as a last resort for children, Victoria and Queensland brought in "adult crime, adult time" laws and nearly all jurisdictions tightened youth bail.

Ms Hunter said she wished the politicians who attended Garma, including NT Chief Minister Lia Finochiarro, had asked the next generation what they thought of the changes.

"There are a whole lot of people here ready to give some solutions, have some discussions, but it just doesn't seem to be happening," she said.

"It would have been nice if [Ms Finochiarro] was able to stay, maybe go into the youth forum and listen to the kids."

The NT government spokesperson said lowering the age of criminal responsibility to 10 was about "early intervention and community safety".

"Strong families, cultural connection and early intervention are the best way to break the cycle of youth crime, alongside clear consequences when offending occurs," they said.

'They are just little kids'

Shanina and Tahni are cousins who love spending time together. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Inside the youth forum, Tahni and Shanina reflected on family and friends who had been caught up in the justice system or removed from their families.

"Those ones that are under Territory Families [in out-of-home-care], they don't know our culture much because they only come once a year for a visit around the community," Shanina said.

"It's hard for them to know who their family is, who they are, and their culture … I feel for them."

The girls say they're worried about the impact of new laws on their family and peers. (ABC News Billy Cooper)

They were also worried about children as young as 10 being held responsible for crimes.

"Ten years old, they're not really teenagers yet, they are just little kids. They aren't mature enough [to understand]," Tahni said.

The cousins share a strong connection with their culture. (ABC News Billy Cooper)

"Instead of sending them away, just discipline them on the island and that way they can learn from their mistakes instead of getting them sent off somewhere else.

"[Juvenile detention is] pretty traumatic, and they'll have to carry that trauma for the rest of their lives."

The cousins say there are deeper issues affecting young people and punishment isn't the solution.

"I think younger children have to do counselling, talk about their feelings … instead of getting frustrated. That causes a lot of problems," Shanina said.

Tahni's message to government is that "our voice matters". (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

As the youth forum began to wind up, Tahni shared her message for the NT government.

"Our voice matters," she said.

"We don't want [Stolen Generations] to happen again.

"If we didn't have culture, we wouldn't know our identity. That's why it's important for us to learn at a young age.

"[Otherwise] there might not be any Tiwi people left. There will just be lost generations."

title: Historic Wattle Park Chalet catches fire on day of scheduled wedding
text:
A historic wedding venue in Melbourne's east that was scheduled to host a reception tonight has erupted in flames, destroying the roof.

Emergency services were called to the Wattle Park Chalet in Surrey Hills about 6:32am this morning, arriving to find the building on fire.

Firefighters brought the blaze under control shortly before 8am, but not before fire, smoke and water damage had devastated much of the main hall.

"The area that's been damaged has been approximately 30 per cent of the building," Fire Rescue Victoria (FRV) incident controller Callum Donoghue said.

Wattle Park Chalet owner Matthew Forsythe has only owned the business for five months, and said he was devastated to see the historic building following the fire.

"It's pretty bad, the damage, certainly when you go inside the hall," he said.

The Wattle Park Chalet in Surrey Hills has been hosting events for almost a century. (ABC News: Sacha Payne)

He said the venue had operated since 1928 and had hosted thousands of weddings.

"This is a tragedy, not just for myself and the bookings I've got, but [for] such a historic building like this to be impacted like this is just horrible to see," Mr Forsythe said.

"I hope at some point in the future we look back and this is just a little speed bump in that history."

Wedding plans thrown into disarray

Mr Forsythe said he had about 20 events planned over the next few months, including a wedding tonight that will need to be relocated.

Mr Forsythe said he was still working to find a replacement venue tonight's reception, admitting he was keeping one half of the couple in the dark about the fire for now.

"We actually haven't told the bride, but I'm dealing with the groom and we're trying to find an alternative venue at the moment that will give them their special day," he said.

"They'll certainly have a story that they'll have to talk about."

A planned wedding at Wattle Park has been forced to relocate after extensive smoke and water damage to the main hall. (ABC News: Sacha Payne)

He said two days of work had gone into preparing for the wedding, with flowers already on the tables and food ready to go.

Mr Forsythe said he was in contact with some other venues to find a suitable replacement for the 110-odd wedding guests.

FRV investigators are yet to determine the cause of the blaze, which impacted the kitchen and service areas of the chalet.

title: Newcastle's finals win is proof the future has come
text:
If Newcastle were going to pull off a classic finals ambush on South Sydney they were going to need some new heroes to be born under the bright lights of the Sydney Football Stadium.

The Knights went into the game light up front, not in size, strength or willingness, but certainly in experience and definitely in recognition. After their 20-10 win over South Sydney, however, they will never have the luxury of being underestimated again.

Across 80 minutes of a classic blood-and-thunder final, fresh faces and young legs won the day as the star-studded Rabbitohs outfit fought on despite being busted until they were finally beaten.

NRL Finals live Newcastle holds on for a 20-10 victory over South Sydney to kick-off the 2026 finals series, but Rabbitohs coach Wayne Bennett fumes at more Bunker confusion after a contentious call.

Perhaps it could have all been different were it not for Cody Walker falling to a sniper's shot early in the second half, suffering a calf injury that ended his night early.

The ageless Walker is what binds the Rabbitohs left edge together and takes it from a series of talented individuals to the closest thing rugby league has to a hammer of the gods.

But you'll find little sympathy for an injury up Newcastle way. They were without Dylan Brown, Dylan Lucas, Trey Mooney and Jacob Saifiti heading into this and while plenty expected them to fight few expected them to win.

After their first finals win away from home in 13 years, expectations be damned. They defied them all over the park, perhaps no more than down their right, where backrower Jermaine McEwan had the game of his young life.

It was always going to be a big night for the 21-year old, one way or the other. It was he who would be tasked with setting up Newcastle's defences against the Rabbitohs knockout left.

He did that with aplomb, even before Walker went down, from setting the tone with driving hits from the inside to holding his width and his nerve when Souths gave their chainsaw a rip.

Throw in two tries and it's the last time McEwan will catch anybody by surprise.

Together that Knights edge put together some of the best defensive plays of the night, but it wasn't the biggest — that honour must belong to McEwan's backrow partner, Francis Manuleleua.

They call him "Big Frisco" and people were put in Alcatraz for the type of violence he dropped on Cameron Murray late in the first half as he raced out of the line to dish out one of the hits of the season.

Technically it was illegal — the shot was clean, but Manuleleua was half a metre offside. The red and blue hordes at the southern end of the ground didn't seem to care, even though Souths scored off the field position, because sometimes it's worth it.

Paying the blood price for a little bit of rough stuff is something Dane Gagai and Latrell Mitchell know well.

The two centres fought like demons after a scuffle midway through the first half and while both won their share of battles it was Gagai who won the war.

Gagai is one of the few older heads in this side — you can call him older but don't call him old, whatever you do — and only a player as sure as himself as the 35-year old would risk poking a bear like Mitchell.

It's something few have done while surviving to tell the tale but Gagai didn't just weather the might and power, he fought like a far younger man, with nothing held back and no regard for his own safety.

His try in the 25th minute was a snapshot the endless love of competition that keeps him young even as the years keep passing and his roar of triumph after he was first to a Sandon Smith kick was among the first harbingers of what was unfolding.

There were other fine battles and contributors — Bradman Best and Jack Wighton, who was close to his side's best, went hell for leather on the other side of the field to Gagai and Mitchell.

Tyson Frizell had a game up front that puts the war back into warhorse and Keaon Koloamatangi left everything out there in his final game as a Rabbitoh.

Kalyn Ponga, once the sun around which everything in Newcastle orbited, was prominent throughout but the class of Smith and Fletcher Sharpe meant the whole game was not on his shoulders and the Knights fullback thrived as a result.

It meant he was able to access the best parts of his game, something the Rabbitohs found difficult throughout even as a torrid defensive effort and several last gasp saves by Campbell Graham kept their heads above water.

They will be haunted by the hypothetical over the summer after their first trip to the finals in four years fell at the first hurdle.

Walker cut a forlorn figure on the South Sydney bench. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

If only Walker didn't get injured, or at least had made it through more of the game.

If only Bud Sullivan's circus act of a try wasn't chalked off for a knock on from Alex Johnston that could have easily been called a strip, just as Dom Young's try could have easily been rubbed off the board.

If only Brandon Smith's last desperate effort with three minutes left — which would have forced a big finish at the very least — didn't come up a blade of grass short.

If only, on a night where they played something resembling their top side for one of the first times all season, they were able to tap into the tried and true talent that lurks somewhere within and rises to the surface enough to tantalise and tease.

They are a team built for the present with stars who made their reputation on tearing down what came before them. That's the law of the jungle and the nature of the game.

The Rabbitohs will fancy their chances of returning to the mix next year but this time around were served a reminder there comes a time when the young feed on the old.

This night was such a time and with nothing to lose and everything to prove, Newcastle was ravenous.

title: Celine Dion returns to stage in Paris after stiff person syndrome diagnosis
text:
Celine Dion will return to the stage this weekend for her first full concert in six years with a sellout Paris residency following her struggles with a rare neurological disorder which sidelined her career.

The singer's return was marked by a giant karaoke celebration in Paris, with fans belting out her classic hits at the Place de la Bataille-de-Stalingrad the night before she took to the stage.

"For me, it's what Paris is all about, just gathering people in open spaces and having a moment together, singing together," Paris resident Suvi Kallom told reporters at the event.

"We know that Celine Dion's concert was a huge popular success. It's difficult to get tickets, many people don't have the pleasure of going," Paris Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said.

"So we try to organise more events focused on fun and sharing a good time."

Fans gathered in Paris to sing Celine Dion's greatest hits together in French. (Reuters: Sarah Meyssonnier )

Celine Dion fans gather as she prepares to perform 26 concerts in Paris. (Reuters: Sarah Meyssonnier)

In 2022, Dion announced in 2022 that she was suffering from stiff person syndrome (SPS) — which causes stiffness and muscle spasms — and disappeared from the limelight.

Since the announcement she has made only one appearance, at the opening ceremony of the 2024 Olympics in Paris where she sang an Edit Piaf song atop the Eiffel Tower.

She is due to perform a series of 26 concerts over the next eight months and draw fans from all over the world.

A sign reads "Let yourself be transported to Celine's concert" at a Paris metro station. (Reuters: Gonzalo Fuentes)

Dion arrived in Paris two weeks ago and fans have waited for hours outside her hotel singing some of her biggest hits.

She even joined them at times.

"She made me dream all my life and I want to thank her," 38-year-old Cristina Piergentili, who travelled from Italy, said outside the Royal Monceau hotel where she hoped to meet the star.

Celine Dion greets fans outside her hotel in Paris. (Reuters: Abdul Saboor )

The metro station at the concert venue has been decorated with some of her most famous lyrics.

Dion told reporters that Paris is her second home.

"She's the greatest, my idol," fan Aurelie Chabroll said as she waited for the singer, known for songs such as My Heart Will Go On, It's All Coming Back To Me Now and Because You Loved Me, outside her hotel.

"She's a fighter. She really proved that to us and her return is just magical."

The first concert of the series will kick off on September 11, local time.

What is stiff person syndrome?

Loading...

SPS is a rare neurological disease with symptoms that include muscle spasms, muscle rigidity, chronic pain and heightened anxiety.

There is no cure for SPS, but there are treatments that can help manage symptoms.

Dion said she was managing her health when she announced the shows in March of this year.

"This year, I'm getting the best birthday gift of my life. I'm getting the chance to see you, to perform for you once again," Dion said.

title: Bendigo, Geelong urged to join light rail revolution
text:
Almost 20 years ago, transport expert and Professor of Sustainability Peter Newman recommended that the City of Greater Bendigo turn its heritage trams into a public transport option.

After three trials over the following months, the city's bosses decided not to adopt it, saying people still preferred their cars.

But now, with light rail making a global resurgence, Bendigo Heritage is proposing the city use light rail to connect key destinations.

The proposal calls for a short city-centre tram route of roughly 1 kilometre linking the Bendigo Station with the retail core and continuing to the Bendigo Art Gallery and Queen Elizabeth Oval precinct.

The proposal also wants trams to run along Barnard Street and connect with the hospital precinct.

The proposed tram route would join the retail, arts, sport and hospital precincts. (Supplied: Bendigo Heritage)

Professor Newman says it is time Bendigo returned to the idea of trams as public transport.

"The communities need to want it, as well as the developers," he said.

"That process should begin straightaway because the opportunities are going to be there.

" The politics is going to be right. These are the areas that people are saying, 'we want to be like the city centres'. "

Two convoys of trams in Pall Mall on September 13, 1970. (Supplied: Bendigo Trust)

Trams ran along Mitchell and View streets until 1972, and the plan by the city's heritage body is to have battery-powered trams traverse that same path.

Bendigo Heritage chief executive James Reade said the resurgence of trams would improve connectivity for Bendigo residents and visitors.

"Their absence is still keenly felt in the character of the city," Mr Reade said.

"We propose a short city centre tram route of roughly 1 kilometre linking the Bendigo Station with the retail core and continuing to the Bendigo Art Gallery and Queen Elizabeth Oval precinct.

"With significant anchors at either terminus, it is a modest line with a mighty job to do."

James Reade says a light rail connection is a major missing piece in Bendigo public transport connectivity. (Supplied: Bendigo Heritage)

The plan would involve reallocating one traffic lane in each of Mitchell Street and View Street to make way for the tram lines and stops.

Figures from the International Association of Public Transport's report on light rail in 2019 showed that, since 2000, more than 100 cities worldwide have opened their first modern light rail line, and light rail now runs in close to 390 cities.

It was found that in Europe more than 210 tram and light rail systems carry billions of passengers a year, and it is the fastest-growing corner of the sector.

Tram revival must meet passenger need

It's not the first time the return of light rail or trams has been proposed as a public transport option in Bendigo.

In 2005, the City of Greater Bendigo scrapped its plan to extend the heritage tram network around Lake Weeroona after the community opposed it.

Three years later, Professor Newman suggested modernising parts of the heritage tram network so it could function as a daily public transport service, but after a week-long trial of trams running every 20 minutes it was not continued.

This week, Professor Newman said Bendigo Heritage's plan was needed to attract private investment and unlock the urban development required to make the tramway a success.

"The right quotient is to bring into the room the people who would be putting money into that project in terms of the urban developments around it and the local, state and federal governments that would be contributing to it," Professor Newman said.

"If you do that, then you'll get an integrated solution rather than a tramway organisation saying, 'Oh, we just like this'.

" This is a proper urban development project that will transform Bendigo if done right. "

Professor Newman backed the idea of battery-powered trams and said Auckland was considering "trackless trams", and there was a proposal for similar to be added to Parramatta Road in western Sydney, while Brisbane's metro used three-carriage battery buses which mirrored a light rail system.

Paul Westcott says Bendigo trams would need to run more frequently to be a useful public transport option. (ABC News: Erin Cooper)

But Public Transport Users Association spokesperson for regional Victoria, Paul Westcott, said light rail would have to run far more frequently than the current hourly heritage tram service along Pall Mall.

"Frequency is always the key to good public transport, not necessarily the mode by which the service is delivered," he said.

"It's pretty clear that if a bus and tram deliver the same frequency on the same route, people would probably prefer a tram.

"But it's not much good putting a tram in unless you are going to provide the level of service and route coverage that is going to be attractive and useful to public transport users."

The Gold Coast has recently added a light rail network to its public transport system. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

'Tram boulevards' for regional cities

The Gold Coast is one of the latest regions to add light rail to its public transport.

The 6.7-kilometre-long Stage 3 of its light rail opened early last month and cost $1.55 billion to build, more than double its initial projection of $709 million.

This week, the G21 conference in Geelong launched its campaign for $12.5 million for the planning and design of a rapid transport corridor between Geelong and the Surf Coast.

At the moment, commuters rely on a 53-minute bus ride to travel the 23 kilometres between the two destinations.

Stretch Kontelj and Libby Stapleton say they are open to transport options between Geelong and Torquay. (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

City of Greater Geelong mayor Stretch Kontelj said trackless trams, or a dedicated rapid bus lane, had already been touted as options.

"I particularly love the sound of trackless trams," he said.

"As they do between Adelaide and Glenelg, that's sort of my vision of how that could potentially work.

"I could see it would be hugely advantageous to people daily for commuting between the two areas, but also a great tourist attraction."

Mr Kontelj said the next stage would be about getting the costings of establishing the transport corridor.

Surf Coast Shire mayor Libby Stapleton said the Surf Coast Highway was already at capacity during peak times, and studies had shown that a business-as-usual approach that relied on cars would not work.

"We know that demand is increasing," she said.

'Cheaper and more accessible'

Ian McBurney has spent 25 years working with communities on sustainable transport and said arriving at Bendigo on the train and catching a tram to the art gallery, Queen Elizabeth Oval and hospital would be a great look for the city.

He said that while the tourism market loves trams, inner-city workers and residents needed a faster and more modern system that ran regularly and got passengers from A to B regularly.

"I'm pretty sure that running ten-minute electric buses would be far cheaper and more accessible," he said.

"Buses can take a lane of the current road, but we would need to build better bus stops. Laying tram tracks would be a complete redesign of the road."

The request for a feasibility study for a new Bendigo tram route has been sent to the Department of Transport and Planning as part of a review into Bendigo's bus network.

title: Patient dies after forgotten referral, Victorian shadow minister says
text:
A patient who was not triaged in a "timely manner" at a Victorian hospital that relies on paper records has died, the state's shadow health minister says.

It is believed up to 150 patients at Mildura Base Public Hospital (MBPH) were left waiting for care for longer than a year after boxes of paper referrals were "forgotten" about.

On Friday Shadow Health Minister Georgie Crozier said she understood that one affected patient had since died.

"[These are] patients that have not been triaged, not been diagnosed, not been seen by specialists and haven't had the management and timely care that they deserve," she told ABC Statewide Drive.

MBPH discovered the fault via clinical governance and patient safety processes and reported the cases to Safer Care Victoria (SCV), in line with its obligations.

MBPH acting chief executive Matt Jukes declined to comment on the forgotten paper referrals, but said the hospital was "always looking at refining our service delivery and models of care".

He said the hospital was working with SCV and the Department of Health "to ensure that if there are any gaps within the services that we provide, that they are identified, they're reviewed".

Matthew Jukes said the hospital is working with Safer Care Victoria to review what happened with the paper documents. (Supplied: Mildura Base Public Hospital)

Records still not digitalised

In 2023 MBPH and the state government committed to digitising 200,000 patient records over four years, with electronic medical records (EMRs) set to roll out in Mildura, Echuca and Swan Hill at a cost of $14 million.

Three years later, Mr Jukes said inpatient records had still not been digitised, and that the hospital needed more funding and time to complete the transition.

"From our perspective, we just work within the constraints of what we have available to us," he said.

In a statement, a Victorian government spokesperson said implementing electronic medical records was "a complex, multi-year transformation" and that the Loddon Mallee EMR program was still underway.

"The Victorian government is progressively rolling out electronic medical records and CareSync Exchange across Victoria's public health system to reduce reliance on paper-based processes and improve access to patient information," they said.

Victoria's shadow health minister says a patient has died after hundreds of paper referrals were "forgotten" in a Mildura hospital. (ABC Mildura-Swan Hill: Christopher Testa)

'Dangerous' system

On Friday, a medical student at the hospital told the ABC the paper system was "dangerous" and that patients were not getting the care they needed.

"We have a paper-based system, hybrid essentially, where doctors, nurses, allied health all scribble down notes," the medical student said, speaking on condition of anonymity.

"We will routinely go on ward rounds and a doctor will run their finger down the length of the paper and say, 'I can't read that. Oh well, next page.'

"It is dangerous, I can't believe that in 2026 we have a paper-based system in Mildura."

The medical student said they understood why some residents were worried about visiting MBPH.

"It's not the staff's fault, [but] if I had something go wrong with me, I'd be jumping in the car and driving to Bendigo," they said.

Victoria falling behind on digitalisation

In 2024 the state government said the rollout of EMRs in all Victorian hospitals was underway.

It is not known how many hospitals are still operating entirely through paper records, but processes differ between them.

In regional Victoria, patients such as Horsham woman Penny Flynn have lost confidence in the system after issues with her health information being missed due to the paper system.

She has resorted to creating her own folders to manage records and appointments.

"It has all my contacts, of all my specialists, all the medications I take and all the people that need to be contacted if I become unwell, and I take that to the specialist with me," Ms Flynn told ABC Victoria Statewide Mornings.

Penny Flynn says she's experienced issues with paper referrals. (Supplied: Penny Flynn)

Australian Medical Association Victorian president Simon Judkins said paper-based hospitals had always been a problem.

"It goes back a long way to individual governance and individual boards and individual health services and so each health service does things their own way," he said.

"There's no systemic or system IT response. We're trying to fix that."

Simon Judkins said regional and rural areas “really need to get up to speed” on digital upgrades. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

Dr Judkins theorised that any potential faults at the Mildura Base may have stemmed from a "high turnover of locum staff who aren't familiar with processes".

"It's a system that … relies on individuals to be aware of how things work, and when those individuals aren't, things like this get missed," he said.

Calls for 'transparent' investigation

Law Partners senior managing solicitor in medical negligence Michael Passaro said the failures reported at MBPH were "deeply disturbing" and called for a 'thorough and transparent' investigation.

Michael Passaro says the matter needs to be probed. (Supplied)

"An urgent referral is not just paperwork, it represents a patient waiting for potentially life-saving care," he said.

" No patient should suffer avoidable harm because their referral was left untriaged in a box. "

The state government spokesperson said their thoughts were with the loved ones of the patients affected.

"When something goes wrong, health services must review what happened, be transparent about the findings and take action to reduce the risk of it happening again," they said.

The ABC understands MBPH has reached out to affected patients.

title: Every month, op-shop owner travels 2,000km into outback to donate clothes
text:
Barbara Carroll loads her van with boxes of donated clothes each month and heads north to the red dirt of Western Australia's remote Pilbara.

The 84-year-old op-shop owner is affectionately known as "Nan Barb" around her home town of Donnybrook, 200 kilometres south of Perth.

Ms Carroll distributes the clothes to charities and women's refuges in places such as Carnarvon, Newman, Nullagine and Roebourne, road trips routinely covering more than 2,000km.

"I don't go out to get any rewards or anything; it just comes naturally," she says.

"Somebody needs help, you help them, and that's what I do.

"They can't just go into a shop and buy clothes. They're too far out."

Her love of country music helps her pass the time on the long drives.

"I'd rather drive by myself. Take me time. I just like it on my own," she says.

Nan Barb regularly travels out to WA's remote communities to distribute clothes. (Supplied: Nan Barb)

Heart in the red dirt

Ms Carroll's community op shop is packed to the hilt with every item imaginable, from old toasters to ornate wedding dresses.

An overabundance of donated clothes from across WA's South West region led her to start the charitable campaign she calls "Nan Goes North".

Nan Barb is on a personal mission to lend a helping hand to remote towns disadvantaged by isolation. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

It is a mission that is close to her granddaughter Tara Carroll's heart.

Tara, who is a proud Wiradjuri woman, joins her grandmother's trips when she can.

"Living remotely, that's a disadvantage already because they don't have access to a lot of medical or clothing or whatever it be," she says.

"So to be able to go with Nan on these adventures with all the clothes and anything that they need, it's pretty cool."

Tara Carroll says her grandmother is an inspiration to her family. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

Nan Barb's personal connection to northern communities runs deep, having been brought up in the remote community of Nullagine, in WA's Pilbara region.

"They are her tribal family; she has a very close connection with people up there, with mob," Tara says.

" Her heart is in the red dirt. "

'We love her'

Shahenaz Kouzi is a community advocate with the Newman-based Puntukurnu Aboriginal Medical Service and former staff member at the local women's refuge.

She said both organisations had regularly received clothes donations from Nan Barb.

The Donnybrook Op Shop donates all sorts of essential clothes for babies, women and men. (Supplied: Nan Barb)

"Blankets, winter and summer clothing, baby clothes, women's and men's clothing, it's tremendous," she said.

"We love her. I wish she was my Nan."

Ms Kouzi said Nan Barb was well-known and loved by residents in the remote communities of the East Pilbara.

"They call her the angel. There are too many good words for Barb from all the Aboriginal people; they all know her," she says.

Nan Goes North

Donnybrook op shop volunteer Andrew Clifford says Nan Barb is a beloved, straight-talking local.

Andrew Clifford says Nan Barb is a local legend around Donnybrook. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

"Oh, she's a lovely lady, does a lot for the community; she's quite funny, very funny," he says.

"The way she speaks and language-wise, it's fairly rough, but it's good."

Despite the occasional mishap on her adventures, Tara Carroll says her nan always manages to find a way home.

"She's been broken down on the sides of the road, and someone always rescues her," Tara says.

" She's got good karma, I believe. "

Ms Kouzi recalls giving Nan Barb eskies full of ice to keep her cool when her van's air conditioning had broken down.

"We worry about her, but she's fit as a fiddle," she said.

Her family and community are raising money for a truck, so Nan Barb can expand her outreach and make it easier to take along a passenger, aside from her dog, Bob.

Nan Barb was raised in the remote WA community of Nullagine. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

"[The van is] too uncomfortable to take two people because there's no room for your legs," Nan Barb says.

"I don't need it, but everybody else reckons I need somebody to go with me."

title: 'Obnoxious' weed woven into massive mullet sculpture
text:
In a suburban garage on the southern Gold Coast, two longtime friends created a supersized fish that is now pride of place at one of Australia's largest outdoor sculpture exhibitions.

It started life relatively small, with the idea of sculpting a piece made entirely of red-nosed, fish-shaped soy sauce packets.

But like so many projects, its scale soon got much bigger.

Ged McCormick hopes the massive mullet inspires others to express themselves through art. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

"We didn't quite think it would be here," said Ged McCormick, who sacrificed half a parking space at his Palm Beach home to bring the sculpture to life.

"We were tossing up doing it at my work or at Rusty's place, but this is just where everything started … and it keeps the neighbourhood entertained."

The concept began as an Indigenous fish trap woven from invasive plants, which the pair planned to fill with fishing line and plastic litter collected from nearby beaches.

Rusty Linnane works on ecological restoration projects, helping transform weed-infested natural areas back to their original condition. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

"Then Ged said, 'How about we do a whole mullet in the style of an Indigenous fish trap,'" co-sculptor, Rusty Linnane, said.

" That's how the process went from me wanting to make a flat piece out of little sushi fish, to 'Let's make a 5-metre mullet!' "

Creating a cat's claw fish

Sold on the idea of a mega-mullet, the next conundrum for the pair was finding a weed strong enough to weave.

Drawing on his experience with ecological restoration projects, Mr Linnane identified cat's claw creeper, a South American species once imported as an exotic ornamental plant, as his target species.

Sushi shop soy sauce packets still feature prominently in the sculpture. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

"It's obnoxious," Mr Linnane said, with a wry smile and a tinge of malice toward the invasive species.

He explained that the yellow-flowered vine's method was to climb a tree and smother it in foliage until it died and crashed to the ground.

"Then it will go to the next tree, and up, and so on and so on," he said.

The mullet is installed on the Currumbin foreshore as part of the 2026 SWELL Sculpture Festival. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby )

With special permission from the state government, Mr Linnane and Mr McCormick were allowed to harvest vines from an infestation in Nerang National Park.

"We started on the edge where we could walk up and see one or two vines going up big trees and we could cut them and treat the bases," Mr Linnane said.

" We were getting lengths of up to 25 to 30 metres, just by selectively picking those vines. "

Rusty Linnane and Ged McCormick wove several kilometres of vine into their mullet sculpture. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

Neither artist could definitively say how many hours they spent harvesting the vines but admitted there were several unplanned trips to collect more material as the mullet began taking shape.

"It would take us about an hour to collect about 125 metres [of usable vine] … and 125 metres does about a 30-centimetre section of the fish," Mr Linnane said.

A SWELL message

After weaving kilometres of vine and stuffing the fish's guts with an almost equal length of discarded fishing line and other plastic litter, Mr Linnane and Mr McCormick moved their creation into place at the annual SWELL Sculpture Festival on the Currumbin foreshore this week.

Discarded fishing line and plastic litter was stitched into a net to create the mullet's stomach. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

SWELL founder and artistic director Natasha Edwards said tens of thousands of people were expected to flood the festival over the next 10 days.

"This year, up to 100 local and international sculptors are transforming the coastline into a spectacular sculpture walk," Ms Edwards said.

"You can walk along barefoot, with the sand between your toes … you're really connecting art and nature together so that the environment and the artworks really speak to each other."

The woven sculpture catches the early morning sun from its vantage point on the Currumbin foreshore. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

Of the many people who catch sight of his co-creation, Mr Linnane hopes at least some of them take the bait on the environmental message it is casting out.

"Don't buy one-use plastics," Mr Linnane said.

" And for every exotic species of plant out there, there's a local native that will do the exact same job, and possibly better. "

Mr McCormick too hopes the mullet gets caught in the mind of those who see it, especially younger generations.

"We're just amateurs, me and Rusty, we're just having fun," he said.

"I guess this shows any kids out there that if you want to express yourself through art, there's always an opportunity to do it."

title: Shelton through to US Open final as he looks to end 23-year drought
text:
American eighth seed Ben Shelton has the chance to end his country's long wait for another men's US Open champion after beating compatriot Frances Tiafoe to reach the final.

Shelton posted a 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 victory over Tiafoe in the second semi-final and will play top seed Alexander Zverev in the final on Monday morning, AEST.

He showed plenty of energy after ousting defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in a quarterfinal match that ended at 3:33 am Wednesday, local time.

It was the latest finish to a match in US Open history.

Andy Roddick was the most recent American to win the men's US Open title, in 2003.

Zverev will play for his second major title this year after beating Karen Khachanov 6-3, 7-6 (9/7), 7-6 (8/6) in the first semi.

Zverev, who had long been considered the best men's player without a major, finally broke through at the French Open this year. The German followed by reaching the Wimbledon final, which he lost to Jannik Sinner, and is 24-2 in grand slam matches this season.

"Sometimes just things go your way and I feel like I've had a lot of struggles at the major level. I was so close so many times and maybe this year God has said that this is going to be your year and just enjoy the time on the court," Zverev said.

Alexander Zverev on his way to a straight-sets win against Karen Khachanov. (Getty Images: Manuela Davies/USTA)

Now he will try to win the title that he still can't believe he let get away in 2020. Zverev won the first two sets against Dominic Thiem but then lost in a fifth-set tiebreaker, as Thiem became the first man to win the US Open title after dropping the first two sets since 1949.

Zverev was solid after going up two sets this time, and has won 13 consecutive sets after becoming the first number one-seeded man to play five-setters in each of the first two rounds of a major.

Khachanov was trying to reach his first major final after a surprising run in New York. He arrived with a losing record for the season but went on to reach his third grand slam semifinal, including second at the US Open.

He started playing better after dropping the first set and then falling behind 2-0 in the second. He finally broke Zverev's serve to tie it and it stayed even until they went to the tiebreaker. The Russian erased Zverev's first two set points in it before Zverev finished it off by winning a 34-shot rally.

Khachanov then had leads of 3-0 and 5-2 in the third-set tiebreaker before Zverev battled back.

title: Growing pains in Rockingham before AUKUS subs even arrive
text:
The arrival of the first AUKUS nuclear submarine and associated personnel is 385 days away and the council is wondering how it will cope with the influx of service people, their families and increased demand on already strained infrastructure.

Even before the arrival of the first Submarine Rotational Force personnel, the area near HMAS Stirling is experiencing strong population growth, Rockingham Mayor Lorna Buchan told 102.5 ABC Perth.

"We're growing by 14 people a day, which is over 5,000 people a year coming to Rockingham without any defence personnel arriving," Ms Buchan said.

"We have to think about the numbers involved within the rotational force coming from the US.

"There will be approximately 1,200 serving personnel arriving over the next four years, and approximately 50 per cent of them will have families."

An average of 14 people a day are moving to the area. (ABC News: Jasmine Hughes)

A report commissioned by the City of Rockingham in 2023 showed roads around Cape Peron were already at capacity, and people had already begun using "rat runs" to get through the traffic.

The area lacks any kind of industrial hub, exacerbating the traffic problem because 70 per cent of the population leave the area to work and study.

Call for greater funding

Ms Buchan said it also meant the city was largely reliant on residential rates income, because the defence facilities within the city were not required to pay rates.

With greater population comes greater demand for council services such as swimming pools and sporting facilities, as well as pressure on services like health care and child care, and increased demand for housing.

Both Ms Buchan and Warwick Carter, the director of Perth South West Metropolitan Alliance, representing six local councils in Perth's southern corridor, would like to see the federal government set up a dedicated fund to support communities that host defence facilities.

Warwick Carter says the region is preparing for activity equivalent to 10 Olympic Games. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

Mr Carter said the influx of defence personnel and workers in defence industries would in turn stimulate the creation of many more jobs, both boosting the economy, and creating pressures on the community.

"We want to keep the quality of life we have down here," he said.

"Can we make sure baristas can still afford to live here? Can we make sure there's enough childcare centres? Can we make sure there's enough retail? Because that's where the growth pressures will be felt.

"We've put a proposal to the federal government saying we should have a fund.

"We've suggested a pilot project of $50 million, not just for our region, but for any defence community in Australia, so places like Wagga, Townsville, they could apply for it as well to put in infrastructure that helps create more resilient communities."

In addition to AUKUS, Mr Carter said there were a number of other projects coming to the region which would both boost the economy and strain existing infrastructure.



"We're tracking about $70 billion worth of government-backed investment coming into the region over the coming decades.

“To put that in context, the Olympic Games in Brisbane is $7 billion, so it's 10 Olympic Games' worth of activity coming to our region."

Amber-Jade Sanderson, who is both WA minister for manufacturing, skills and TAFE and minister assisting the minister for defence industries, said the state government had already provided support and would provide more in the future.

Amber-Jade Sanderson says local schools and the hospital are being upgraded. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

"There's significant support already going into the community and we're always looking at how we can support more," Ms Sanderson said.

"They've been provided around $20 million worth of funding from the state government for sporting facilities, including their aquatic centre and the basketball centre.

"We're upgrading local schools. We're providing a new mental health emergency centre for Rockingham Hospital. We're starting the work around that redevelopment of Rockingham Hospital."

Local training hopes

The other need local leaders identify as urgent is for more training to be available locally for all the skilled jobs that will be created in defence and associated industries.

Ms Buchan said the Rockingham campus of Murdoch University, which has not hosted students since 2014, should be reopened, as well as a skills centre in Rockingham.

"We need that [campus] pulled out of mothballs. That will need significant investment from the state government to help that happen," she said.

AUKUS is set to transform Rockingham from a quiet beachside outer suburb into a much busier place. (ABC News: Rhiannon Shine)

Ms Sanderson said she was looking at a range of ways to train the workforce the state would need in the future.

"We'll be releasing the Workforce Development Plan later this year, which is an industry-based plan for the resources sector, defence, creative skills and industry, manufacturing, clean energy," she said.

"We need every industry to lean in and invest in apprentices, invest in training, support school leavers with school-based traineeships and apprentices and make sure that they're getting opportunities.

"I agree with the mayor that we do need the skills centre here."

Ms Sanderson said despite the challenges, local communities should welcome the investment that AUKUS would bring.

"This is a beautiful place to live and work and that's why so many people are coming to this area," she said.

"It's not necessarily because of the AUKUS program or the naval shipbuilding, but to inject that amount of investment in the local economy should be welcomed by the local government and local businesses.

"We're going to give them opportunities that just would not have been presented if this had not been happening."

title: Rio Tinto's exit from remote NT town looms large over by-election
text:
Rio Tinto's impending withdrawal from the Gove Peninsula is looming large over a remote by-election in the Northern Territory.

Production at the mining giant's north-east Arnhem Land bauxite mine will stop in 2029 — a second blow for Nhulunbuy after its alumina refinery shut in 2014.

The town's future without its largest employer is the focus of today's Mulka by-election, triggered by the resignation of 10-year independent MLA Yiŋiya Guyula.

Yiŋiya Guyula resigned from NT parliament last month, triggering a by-election. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Mr Guyula quit suddenly last month, citing an inability to work with a Country Liberal Party (CLP) government he claimed was "not willing to listen or form partnerships with Aboriginal communities".

Only a Labor and independent candidate are seeking to replace Mr Guyula, with the CLP choosing not to run in a seat the party has not held since 1980.

Mulka is a former safe seat for Labor, until former deputy leader Lynne Walker lost to Mr Guyula by eight votes in 2016.

Yiwarr McGrath, a former NT Young Australian of the Year and trailblazing nurse, was preselected by the party last month and said the region had been forgotten.

Yiwarr McGrath is the Labor contender for the seat of Mulka. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"The CLP government has neglected this part of the world — how do we have ongoing sustainability around housing, healthcare," he said.

"I've been listening — I'm going to bring those issues to the table so [the government] is aware of what's going on post-mining.

" I'm from Mulka, I am Yolŋu, I grew up here, I know the issues here — I've been through poverty — I'll bring real experience and embed practicality. "

Although it is not running a candidate, Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro has said the CLP is committed to the future of Nhulunbuy, which is also losing its major supermarket, Woolworths, next year.

At the Garma Festival in July, Mrs Finocchiaro announced the town's lease would be handed to the Rirratjingu clan after Rio Tinto's exit, and also called for greater fuel security in the region.

Andrew Blamey is running as an independent, saying the two-party system is not working. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Independent candidate Andrew Blamey said he was running in the by-election after coming to the view that politics in the NT was "broken".

"The two-party system is failing us," he said.

" Independent voices in the parliament are very important to get people's views spoken about. "

A Territorian for almost 20 years and a Nhulunbuy resident for three, Mr Blamey said while in government, Labor had dropped the ball on the town's transition.

"I think it's important to remember that Rio Tinto announced they were leaving the area in 2019," he said.

Yirrkala residents have already begun voting in the by-election for the remote seat of Mulka. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"Labor were in power for [eight] years until 2024.

"I feel we need to move away from the blame game and a lot of voters are saying that to me as well.

"They want real answers and outcomes."

Long-standing issues remain

Just south of Nhulunbuy in Yirrkala, Laynhapuy Homelands Aboriginal Corporation vice-chair Barayuwa Munuŋgurr said overcrowded homes remained a key issue in the region's Aboriginal communities.

Barayuwa Munuŋgurr says overcrowding is an issue in remote communities. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"We need more houses, to get the wellness and wellbeing of our people, the same, because I feel that health comes first, with housing," he said.

"We have issues with diabetes, kidney failures, it's due to overcrowding and not enough housing."

Yirrkala resident Charles Yunupiŋu said he was living with his family in a home where he shared one room between five people.

"It is really frustrating for everyone, it's difficult for everyone to sleep," he said.

Charles Yunupiŋu says north-east Arnhem Land needs more skills training for young people. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Mr Yunupiŋu said the region also needed more skills training for young people.

"We need people to jump on work — most people just walk around and do nothing, you know, it's a bit sad too actually," he said.

"We need to help people to build their future for the next generation."

Arian Pearson, a sound designer and studio engineer based in Yirrkala, said tourism should be a major part of the region's plan post-mining.

Arian Pearson says Yirrkala needs more space for tourists to park their vehicles. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"We need to build infrastructure to enable people to come to these communities and to support the community economically," he said.

"The visitors that come here need somewhere to stay.

"There's an influx of people that come in — campers, caravaners — that need more space to be able to park their vehicles.

"Tourism is a major factor economically for the region, so putting that infrastructure in place is needed for people to enjoy it."

Meanwhile, Mr Pearson's partner Ruth Pearson said a lack of day care in Yirrkala was impacting her ability to work.

Ms Pearson said high staff turnover at the day care centre run by the East Arnhem Regional Council had led to several closures over the past five years.

Ruth Pearson says the local day care centre in Yirrkala has been closed since July and is not set to reopen until October. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

She said the centre had been closed since July and was not set to reopen until October.

"I get paid for the hours that I work, so I've been missing out on hours," she said.

Yiŋiya Guyula resigns, labelling CLP policies 'dehumanising' The independent member for Mulka, Yiŋiya Guyula, has resigned from NT parliament effective immediately.

"Over 300 hours this year that I could not go to work because the day care centre has been closed, which is over $12,000 in wages that I could not earn.

"My husband has a massive family in this community and yes, we have a lot of family members that can help care for our kids, but they all work, they are all in jobs, so I need help during work hours."

Ms Pearson also said her household was paying $5,300 in rates to the council each year.

"We are not a high-income family, so for us these rates mean every year we don't go away for Christmas," she said.

"Every year, we save up, we save up, we save up and then comes the end of the year and we get the rates bill and those savings go into the rates bill."

title: The ‘unique’ Docker standing between the Swans and another grand final
text:

Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 The ‘unique’ Docker standing between the Swans and another grand final Jonathan Drennan September 12, 2026 — 1:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After completing an intense week of training on Friday afternoon, Swans players were divided on what to do that evening. Some wanted to watch the semi-final between Fremantle and Geelong, which would determine their opponent in next weekend’s preliminary final. Others were happy to tune out of footy for the night and wait until they reconvened to begin the forensic analysis of their next match. The Swans who did tune in to the Dockers’ tense 14-point victory at Optus Stadium were treated to an exceptional performance from ruckman Luke Jackson, with the onus now shifting to how to stop him at the SCG. Loading Swans coach Dean Cox, one of the AFL’s greatest ever ruckmen, will be aware that if Sydney can nullify Jackson, another grand final is possible. Jackson was a key man in Fremantle’s minor premiership, but the Dockers are by no means a one-man band. Jackson was joined on this year’s All-Australian team by four teammates: Shai Bolton, Jordan Clark, Murphy Reid and Josh Treacy. Against the Cats, Bolton was outstanding, kicking two goals and finishing with 26 disposals. But it was Jackson who flipped the game.

Advertisement

With five minutes left of the third quarter, Fremantle had conceded three successive goals and their home crowd was tense. Jackson, a former Australian under-17 basketball star, finished the quarter with eight disposals, two goals, four score involvements and 12 hitouts. In their previous meeting this season, in Perth in July, the Swans held a two-point lead at the end of the third quarter before Fremantle kicked nine goals in the final term to win by 38 points and underline their premiership credentials. Luke “the Unicorn” Jackson was nothing short of brilliant for the Dockers. AFL Photos In that game, Swans ruckman Brodie Grundy had 29 hitouts to Jackson’s 26, with Fremantle also able to utilise Mason Cox, who had 10 hitouts. The Swans do not have a deputy with the experience of Cox, having recently used forward Hayden McLean to relieve the veteran Grundy at stoppages. Grundy’s dominance has been a foundation of Sydney’s finals run, but against Jackson in the preliminary final he will face one of the biggest tests of his career. Grundy cannot match Jackson’s scoring threat, with the Fremantle ruck averaging a goal a game and finishing the season with 27 majors, a rarity for his position.

Advertisement

But in the core skill of hitouts, Grundy averages 34.3 a game compared to Jackson’s 25.7. Grundy also possesses an ability to act as an auxiliary midfielder when needed and will need to do so to curb Jackson’s influence. The Swans’ midfield trio of James Rowbottom, Jai Serong and Errol Gulden combined beautifully in their qualifying win against Brisbane to help dominate clearances, but a lot of their success came through Grundy’s dominance at stoppages. Brodie Grundy tussles with Luke Jackson in the last meeting between the sides, in Perth in July. AFL Photos via Getty Images Grundy’s presence in the Swans side has transformed their ability to score from clearances. According to Champion Data, no player has averaged more hitouts-to-advantage at centre bounces than Grundy (3.9) since 2024. From retail workers and Uber Eats drivers to martial arts masters and cosmetic surgeons, Sydney’s council chambers are filled with elected officials juggling a range of jobs.

Mayors and councillors at the state’s 128 local councils are not paid full-time wages but receive fees determined by the Local Government Remuneration Tribunal. Those payments are determined by the size and type of council on which they serve. For example, a City of Sydney councillor is paid between $32,810 and $48,140. Northern Beaches councillor Jody Williams is a trade lane gatekeeper three days a week at Bunnings, where he loads cars and checks receipts – and the community’s pulse. Northern Beaches councillor Jody Williams keeps an eye on the local economy by working at Bunnings. Lane Cove Labor councillor David Roenfeldt drives buses from Sydney Airport to Yass and Canberra, while Bayside Council’s Chris Saravinovski, also Labor, works as an airport ramp agent, and is a jack-of-all-trades from baggage handling to health and safety. title: Dust-up over new quarry divides coastal town that’s become a hit with tourists
text:
Advertisement

NationalVictoriaMining Dust-up over new quarry divides coastal town that’s become a hit with tourists Benjamin Preiss September 12, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Atop the rolling hills of Fish Creek, the panoramic South Gippsland coast stretches out below in stunning glory. The Strzelecki Ranges, Wilsons Promontory, Corner and Shallow inlets are among the world-class landscapes that greet both travellers and locals alike. For more than 30 years, this treasured landscape has drawn in residents and small-scale farmers who have built homes and livelihoods within Fish Creek’s lush green hills. Plans for a new quarry, nearby an existing pit, have sparked concerns among residents in Fish Creek. Eddie Jim But soon, the view may also include a gaping hole in the ground, with plans to build a new quarry among the idyllic farmland triggering alarm in the community amid concerns about dust, noise and environmental damage. But the operator, which runs an existing mudstone quarry on the same parcel of farmland, insists it is aiming to address legitimate concerns through good design and appropriate operating controls.

Advertisement

Fish Creek Quarries says it is planning to begin constructing a new quarry near its existing pit, which is reaching the end of its life. The current quarry produces primarily mudstone and shale rock, which is typically used for farm tracks, laneways and access roads. Richard Gange is among the residents who fear the proposed quarry will be harmful to the environment and their health. Having bought his property, which neighbours the quarry, about 30 years ago, Gange has raised his three daughters there together with his wife. “It’s catastrophic for us,” he said of the proposed quarry works, which will be metres from his house.

Advertisement

Gange said he has watched the existing quarry grow from a small operation several decades ago into a large worksite with frequent truck movements. While tree planting and the deep level of the existing quarry helped mitigate some dust and noise over the years, he said the new plans ignited fears locally about exposure to crystalline silica dust, which can result in the lung disease silicosis. Land surrounding the quarry had also been subdivided, he said, which had brought a higher population density to the area and made resource extraction no longer appropriate in the Fish Creek hills. Richard Gange and his wife Sita Morton at the Fish Creek property overlooking Wilsons Promontory. Eddie Jim “This is not a small quarry,” he said. “The town has changed. We’re a tourist destination now.” Oil producer and Golden Creek Olives co-owner Rima O’Sullivan said the new quarry would loom over her farm, which is home to about 1000 olive trees, and she fears dust from the proposed resource extraction could contaminate her oil production process.

Advertisement

“It’s windy here,” she said. “There’s no doubt the dust is going to blow off that hill.” O’Sullivan said the quarry currently produced little noise because it was surrounded by trees and workers were quarrying deep beneath the surface, but the new proposed site would decapitate a large hill and kick up dust plumes. Rima O’Sullivan at her olive farm. Eddie Jim “We’re not anti-quarry,” O’Sullivan said. “It’s just too close to housing and businesses.” The proposed extraction site is 17.3 hectares within a broader work authority area of almost 50 hectares.

Advertisement

Fish Creek Quarries spokeswoman Emma Hicken said the company intended to finish operations in the current pit and then move into the new extraction site. “This will allow us to continue supplying an important local source of mudstone and shale, while also allowing us to progressively rehabilitate the existing pit,” she said. A view of the proposed quarry site with a vineyard below. Eddie Jim Hicken said the early stages of proposed pit would be positioned so it was largely hidden within the surrounding landscape. However, the new quarry will be significantly bigger than the existing pit if it proceeds. Friends of the Earth’s Strzelecki Koala Collective has also lashed plans for the new quarry, arguing the farmland earmarked for the extraction site provided a “highway” for native wildlife to the nearby Hoddle Range Flora Conservation Reserve.

Advertisement

Hicken said concerns about koalas should not be dismissed, but said the proposed pit had been designed without removal of native vegetation. She said further planting could create additional habitat. However, an existing windbreak consisting of trees planted by the quarry property owner would need to be removed as part of the proposal. Related Article Victorian election ‘We are not banjo-playing dimwits’: The deep rural resentment that will shape the election Hicken also acknowledged the presence of crystalline silica in the quarry materials, but said the company was working with environmental and regulatory authorities to minimise dust impacts. “Our focus is on preventing dust where we can, controlling it at the source and making sure the right monitoring and management measures are in place.” South Gippsland Shire chief executive Allison Jones said the council had not received any planning permit applications for the site. Before the quarry operator can lodge an application with the council, it must first obtain the required licences from the state government.

Advertisement

Resources Victoria said it had not yet received an application for a new quarry at Fish Creek. However, a spokesman for the agency said it had approved 10 new quarry licences, known as work authorities, during the 2025-26 financial year. Kim Kemper is among the residents worried about the new quarry in Fish Creek. Eddie Jim Kim Kemper is among the locals struggling with the stress of uncertainty about exactly when or if the new quarry will proceed. The proposed work authority is about 20 metres from her property’s boundary, and about 50 metres from her house. Kemper said it was impossible to plan for the future with the prospect of a massive quarry next door. “We’re in limbo,” she said. “I hate it.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.
