title: The Roosters’ wheels came off at exactly the wrong time. Can they go back to the future?
text:
Advertisement

Analysis SportNRLNRL 2026 The Roosters’ wheels came off at exactly the wrong time. Can they go back to the future? Dan Walsh September 12, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In the “before time” of four weeks ago, when Sam Walker still roamed the field without a moon boot, the Roosters were premiership favourites. As James Tedesco notes, you don’t exactly forget “the best defensive performance of your season”. Loading The Tricolours’ stirring 12-6 upset of Penrith on August 13 wasn’t just their most recent victory. It was the club’s biggest win in years, finally shaking the chokehold Ivan and Nathan Cleary had held them in – to the tune of an 11-1 record – in the six-again era. They rattled Nathan like never before, regularly rushing up on the champion No.7 given Isaah Yeo was sidelined, shutting down Penrith’s attack with goal line defence (occasionally illegal) that harked back to their halcyon 2018-19 premiership-winning days.

Advertisement

Ten days later, the Roosters lost to the Tigers. They’re still yet to fully recover. Walker went down the following week against the Dolphins, and Trent Robinson chose to cut his losses and rest nine of his best players for the local derby against the Rabbitohs, which they lost by 30. That Panthers breakthrough capped an eight-game winning run, in which they conceded a miserly 12.8 points a game (the best record of any side over that period). The rhythm that went out the window in a bludging Sunday afternoon, 25-24 loss to the Tigers briefly returned against the Dolphins a week later.

Advertisement

But both losses were set up by alarming defensive lapses – the kind Penrith have taken and beaten teams senseless with for years now. The Roosters coughed up three tries between the 19th and 26th minutes to the Tigers – two down their right edge and another directly from a fumbled pass on their own line. The Roosters were premiership favourites just a month ago. NRL Imagery The Dolphins peeled off three tries in nine minutes before half-time, targeting Daly Cherry-Evans and Rob Toia’s suspect decision-making on the Roosters’ left. “When things don’t go our way, we’ve struggled to get back to what we do well,” Tedesco says – having been sidelined (and rested) for all bar the Dolphins game in the past month.

Advertisement

“We can’t let things snowball, and in those games, one bad thing has led to another. So I think that’s on me as captain and the leaders to help fix that up against Penrith. Things aren’t always going to go perfectly. But you can’t let that slide for 15-20 minutes either. You have to move onto the next job and recover.” How the Roosters’ attack recovers without the enigmatic Walker and adjusts to the probable scrum-base combination of Daly Cherry-Evans and Hugo Savala is key. “Maybe they become a little more structured,” champion playmaker and ex-Roosters halves coach Cooper Cronk says. “Maybe they [adopt] a little bit more of a set-play mentality – play one, two, three [settling plays] and then play off the back of that.

Advertisement

“Sam Walker’s effectiveness is his unpredictability. Maybe the Roosters narrow that down a bit and start doing a little bit of sequence play to get the best out of Savala and Cherry-Evans.” The returns of Victor Radley (concussion), Daniel Tupou (back last week from a lengthy shoulder injury) and Angus Crichton (broken foot) can’t be overstated. Can Daly Cherry-Evans get the Roosters’ campaign back on track? James Brickwood The Roosters attack was the definition of clunky against the Tigers. Without Radley holding them together in the middle, and then understandably when rocked by Walker’s injury, they were listless for much of the Dolphins clash too. For all their attacking wares, the Roosters haven’t been that flash attacking from inside the opposition’s 20-metre zone all season.

Advertisement

But the 43 tackles they had pressing the Tigers’ line, and 38 doing the same from inside the Dolphins’ 20, should have been enough to win both matches by their standards. The Roosters have still scored the most tries from kicks (33) of any team this season. But of late, one of their best attacking weapons has been holstered – Rex Bassingthwaighte’s 79th-minute try against the Rabbitohs last week was their first from the boot in a month. Recent form, pundits, punters and the bookies alike give the Bondi-based side little hope against the Panthers. The Penrith juggernaut does seem to be rolling once more, with Yeo back in the middle and Cleary as imperious as ever. But Robinson and the Roosters have been here before – losing back-to-back games late in their 2013 and 2018 premiership runs, with a 2013 upset loss to the Gold Coast especially memorable given the Titans were $12 outsiders at kick-off.

Advertisement

And even without main man Walker, the Roosters still boast an array of talent and firepower that most NRL rivals could only dream of. And they know it. “We know we’ve got the X-factor to compete with anyone,” Tedesco says. “And especially against Penrith, you can’t hold back or play too safe. But we have to be ready to do the tough things first, and that starts with our defence and our kick-chase – doing those little things right will earn us the chance to play our style of footy and then put some pressure on them.”

title: ‘One tough kid’: Boy, 15, found after days clinging to capsized boat in frigid water off Alaska

WorldNorth AmericaAlaska ‘One tough kid’: Boy, 15, found after days clinging to capsized boat in frigid water off Alaska John Seewer September 12, 2026 — 1:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Toledo, Ohio: A 15-year-old boy survived on top of an overturned skiff in Alaska’s frigid Bering Sea for about two days, losing his older brother and then his cousin to the ocean after the boat capsized while they were out fishing. The teen, identified by a relative as Derek Parker Aghnaanga, was finally hoisted to safety by a fishing boat near St Lawrence Island – a remote Alaskan island closer to Russia than it is to the United States. The bodies of his cousin and brother were also recovered. Loading The cousin had held on to the overturned boat for a while too, but did not survive to be rescued, the teen told one of the rescuers. The captain of the fishing boat that came to his aid said Aghnaanga clung to the skiff through darkness and water temperatures about 10 degrees Celsius.

Advertisement

“That’s one tough kid,” Adam White, captain of The Northwest Explorer, told KTUU-TV in Anchorage. “Through teeth chattering, he had mentioned that his brother was still under the skiff,” White said. “And then he said that, in the previous night, before our rescue, that his cousin had slipped away.” Derek Parker Aghnaanga, 15,was pulled to safety from the overturned hull of his skiff by the crew of a fishing vessel. Rob Suryan/NYT US Coast Guard planes and helicopters spotted the skiff on Monday after family members reported the three missing the night before. The group left the village of Savoonga on St Lawrence Island last Friday and planned to return early Sunday, the Coast Guard said. Halibut fishing is a part of the culture and important to survival in the village where there are about 800 residents and jobs are hard to come by, said Collen Walker, an aunt of the brothers. Residents often share their catch with family and neighbours, she said.

Advertisement

“That’s how we do it in our community. We take care of one another,” she said. “We still live a traditional way of life even if the world is changing.” Aghnaanga, the teen rescued, often went fishing with his 35-year-old brother, Sidney Kulowiyi, and looked to him as a father figure ever since their own father died when they were younger, Walker said. A fishing boat came to the stranded teen’s aid after he was spotted. Carlos Alexis Escartin via AP She described Kulowiyi, a commercial fishing captain, as a humble and loving “provider for people in the village”. She didn’t want to release the name of their cousin who died, saying he also came from Savoonga. Their skiff capsized Saturday night far out in the ocean, she was told.

Advertisement

The Coast Guard said one of its aircrews spotted the boy Monday morning and deployed a raft and supplies before contacting The Northwest Explorer. Aghnaanga’s mother was listening to a radio transmission of the rescue on Monday while other family members huddled around a speakerphone, Walker said. “We all cried and jumped for joy when the captain announced on the radio, ‘We found a kid, he’s alive, he’s alive,’” she said. “Then we asked, ‘Where’s the rest of them?’” Video of the rescue shows Aghnaanga in a bright yellow jacket kneeling atop the overturned skiff. The boat’s crew tosses him a line, tugging the skiff closer until they can pull him into a rescue basket.

Advertisement

He was experiencing symptoms of hypothermia when he got onto the boat, the Coast Guard said. The fishing boat crew warmed him with blankets and hot packs, its captain said. The Queensland government’s wage bill is set to jump a further $93 million this financial year, after the industrial umpire ordered a 4.75 per cent lift to award rates and allowances. The Queensland Industrial Relations Commission decision on the 2026 State Wage Case, published late on Friday, ultimately mirrored its federal counterpart’s July call. Unions had sought the 4.75 per cent rise, which the state conceded would be hard to “argue strongly” against despite warning of the pressure such a rise would put on its $40 billion wages bill. The increase will apply to some specific awards, but will also flow wider into the public sector, including to some workers who were unlikely to have otherwise seen a pay rise this year. Matt Dennien The decision also follows Queensland’s first credit rating downgrade in almost two decades over “weaker budgetary performance”, putting even more pressure on the Crisafulli government.

The 4.75 per cent lift will apply to awards largely used for staff of First Nations councils, Parents and Citizens Associations, and auxiliary firefighters, but will also flow wider into the public sector. This is because a range of collective agreements between much of the sector and the state include clauses to ensure their wages are not below those set in the relevant award. The state ultimately put its position that given the prevailing economic conditions, the industrial context, and all the information before the Full Bench, it would be a difficult task for the state to “argue strongly” against a 4.75% increase. QIRC 2026 State Wage Case decision In documents filed as part of the case, Treasury put this figure at up to 29 of the state’s collective agreements – including six that are in arbitration – with a total cost of $93 million across 2026-27. title: From ‘faster, higher stronger’ to ‘bolder, shorter, louder’ – athletics takes a great leap
text:
Advertisement

SportAthleticsOlympics Opinion From ‘faster, higher stronger’ to ‘bolder, shorter, louder’ – athletics takes a great leap Michael Gleeson Sports columnist September 12, 2026 — 12:15pm

September 12, 2026 — 12:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The black cat analogy wittily describes the differences between religion and science. Philosophy, thus, is like being in a dark room looking for a black cat. Metaphysics is being in a dark room looking for a black cat that isn’t there, while theology is being in a dark room looking for a black cat that isn’t there and shouting, “I’ve found it”. Usain Bolt has lent his star power to World Athletics Ultimate Championships. Getty Images Sport, as a modern religion, has this week joined the analogous spectrum, coming in after metaphysicians. Sports administrators are blind people in a dark room looking for a black cat that might or might not be there but figure if they make themselves smaller and use TikTok the cat will come to them. This week against the backdrop of the NFL – America’s biggest, brashest sport – liberating a new foreign land, other sports were wondering how they got bigger, brasher and brassier? But mainly bigger. It can’t be all Tay Tay and Travis Kelce.

Advertisement

New national tennis honcho Andrew Abdo floated the idea of cutting early matches at the Australian Open back to three sets, an idea quickly put back in the bottle by Tennis Australia. Abdo is a former NRL guy. The organisation he now leads runs the Australian Open, which these days has so many people queuing to get in they’ve stretched it out over even more days. Abdo wouldn’t be the first administrator to suggest more event, less sport. New AFL chairman Craig Drummond has leafed through the same sport marketing playbook. Footy with a new Tassie team coming in will mean a longer season. They could have a shorter one (as if) and play each other once. That would satisfy integrity concerns over a compromised fixture. But they won’t do that. They’ll schedule more games but make them shorter. The NFL brought its unrivalled pizazz to the MCG on Friday. Getty Then Cricket Australia this week decided its shortest version T20, introduced as the panacea for Test cricket’s shortcomings, or longcomings as it turns out, was so good they would invite private owners to spend their millions on Big Bash League teams. England cricket, meanwhile, had previously decided that making cricket shorter was such an effective ploy they would double down and make it shorter still. They introduced The Hundred. It goes for 100 balls. If they could distil it to an over and run it as an ad break they might. T20 was soooo long and boring. This in a country where Great Rail Journeys vies with Midsomer Murders for entertainment.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 The NRL is a one-man band. The AFL is not. Both codes are open to a rebellion Roy Masters Sports Columnist Which brings us to this weekend in Hungary. Athletics, a sport that has to scream to be heard outside of the Olympics every four years and, at a pinch, during the bi-annual World Championships, has sallied forth into this brave new world of reinvention. On Friday in Budapest, the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship was launched. It’s a title that sounds like it’s aimed at the professional wrestling market. The event is a drastically cut-back, invitation-only all-stars version of the World Championships. Essentially, it’s an abridged major competition to fill a hole in the calendar in the off-years when there are no World Championships. But it looks nothing like a regular championship.

Advertisement

Firstly, it goes for three night sessions of three hours each, instead of nine days of morning and night sessions. So that means a heap of events miss out, some mercifully so, but each night has at least one throwing event and one jumping. There are no heats and fewer rounds. There are 28 finals, with straight finals held in all field events as well as the 800m, 1500m and the 5000m. The shorter distance races will have no heats and only two semi-finals. Sprinter Noah Lyles has backed the Ultimate Championships but isn’t fit enough to compete. Getty Images “The Ultimate will not follow a conventional timetable but rather a show script in which every second is accounted for. Scenario-planning between broadcast and event presentation ensures that moments of surprise and delight are captured and that no storyline will be missed,” World Athletics said. “The championship programme was developed with a television audience at its heart, allowing for more storytelling around the athletes, while also engaging fans more effectively through digital platforms.” It sounds like it will have the curated reality of an episode of Alone.

Advertisement

The infield is black to literally block out distracting action when events are not on and athletes are not competing, meaning each event is spotlighted. Not just that: “A bespoke sound identity will reflect the vibe and energy of the Ultimate brand, with pole vault world record-holder Mondo Duplantis in charge of delivering the Ultimate Anthem.” If you have any idea what that word salad means you might win a medal. Well, you might … if The Ultimate issued them. The athletes at this event will not compete for medals, they’ll vie for a share of the $US10 million in prizemoney – each winner will get $150k and a quirky, as yet unrevealed, trophy. For the record, the Ultimate Anthem is the song Duplantis wrote and sang for the event. You read that right.

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

NFL 2026 Singing, cheering and an American takeover: Why the NFL’s MCG experiment was a smash hit This is part of the unashamed attempt to engage and use the biggest names in the sport to decide what the event should look like how to make the sport better. It is arguably a smarter approach than asking only marketeers, broadcasters or influencers. So Usain Bolt, still the biggest figure in the sport, years after retiring as the greatest athlete ever, is helping curate the event. Noah Lyles, the current sprint champion and showman, has been consulting on how to crank the in-stadium, on-TV, hype and excitement. Sadly, consulting will be as close as he gets because he injured himself last month and had to pull out of competition. Tennis-style on-court interviews are being held with athletes in the stadium. The push, post the success of TV’s Drive to Survive, is to leverage the personality of the athletes, not the athletics, to engage new audiences. So all athletes will immediately be given access to footage and photos of themselves competing to push on their digital channels and social media. It will create a circular marketing tool for sport and athlete. The danger some sports have found showcasing the “real person” is discovering the athlete is as interesting as hydronic heating.

Advertisement

Fortunately, athletics has some with spunk, hence, despite not automatically qualifying, Jakob Ingebrigtsen and Josh Kerr will both race the mile. Really, they couldn’t not be there. They are the hottest head-to-head race in the world right now. Norwegian Jakob Ingebrigsten is one of the stars on show at the Ultimate Championships. AP Photo/Beata Zawrzel Ingebrigtsen, the Norwegian punk with a boy-band hairstyle, tatts and good looks, is not only imperiously quick and one of the best the world has ever seen, he is also one of the most cavalier and indiscreet interviewees in sport. It is not just Scandinavian bluntness, he simply could not give fewer f---s. Like Lyles, Sha Carri Richardson and Mondo Du Plantis, Ingebrigtsen is box office. He had to be there. The reigning Olympic champions are all automatically invited, as are the reigning world champions and the Diamond League winners and the organisers retain discretion in the invitation-only event to make sure the athletes people actually want to see are featured.

Well, this is a kind of Nitro Two. Ultimate Nitro? It looks like it could be a bit like Nitro … only better and sustainable. The NRL has backed two crucial officiating decisions that went against South Sydney in their 20-10 loss to Newcastle that prompted Rabbitohs coach Wayne Bennett to call for the bunker to be abolished. Bennett blasted the NRL bunker after a knock-on ruling against Alex Johnston denied the Rabbitohs a try at a vital stage during their elimination final defeat, declaring: “The quicker they get rid of the bunker, the happier I’ll be.” Loading There was also conjecture about the bunker’s decision to green-light a Knights try 10 minutes later when winger Dominic Young was deemed not to have put a foot on the sideline despite several angles suggesting his boot had touched the chalk. However, head office was comfortable with both calls after a thorough post-game review, according to sources who are aware of the verdict but not authorised to comment.

Advertisement

The tough calls aside, South Sydney were struggling when they lost Cody Walker to a calf injury just before half-time. They then lost to an impressive Knights side, who march on to week two of the finals for a showdown against the loser of Saturday afternoon’s Warriors-Dolphins clash. Approaching the hour mark at Allianz Stadium on Friday night, Latrell Mitchell squeezed a pass for Johnston who appeared to have the ball stripped from him by Knights back-rower Jermaine McEwen. Did Jeremaine McEwen strip the ball from Alex Johnston? Nine Play was allowed to continue and Johnston kneed the ball forward, then Jayden Sullivan kicked it further ahead before scoring. Referee Ashley Klein awarded a try, but bunker official Chris Butler had other ideas, claiming McEwen had been trying to make a tackle and that Johnston had lost the ball.

Advertisement

Instead of levelling the scores at 10-10 with a kick to come, Souths were put on the back foot – and 10 minutes later conceded a try to Young, who appeared to put his right foot on the touchline. The bunker is only required to uphold an on-field decision if there is inconclusive or insufficient evidence for it to make its own clear, independent determination. It means that the off-field official shouldn’t default to the referee’s original call, regardless of how fine the margin is. Which is why both contentious rulings ultimately went in the Knights’ favour. Loading Bennett complimented Newcastle on playing a “tremendous game”, and was mindful to not deflect from the result, but he was also frustrated with the bunker, which was established to eliminate contentious calls. “Anyone who plays rugby league or knows rugby league knows that was a knock-on,” Bennett said. “The ball was knocked out of his [Johnston’s] hands. The referee awards a try, then the bunker buys in and says it’s no try.

Advertisement

Cody Walker hobbles off with a calf injury. NRL “Ten minutes later, Newcastle winger Dom Young goes down the sideline, I’m not sure if he put his foot on the sideline, but the bottom line is the bunker comes back and says, ‘We’re going with the referee’s call’. “I want to know who is refereeing the game, that’s the first thing I want to know. Is it the bunker or is it the referee? “In the case of Alex Johnston ... you can look at that 50 times, everyone can come up with a different opinion. It’s just too technical. It’s not what the game needs. “I’ve been in the game a long time, I’ve seen a lot of things, and I don’t think the bunker enhances our game to the [level] we believe it does.”

Advertisement

Bennett said he was happy to live with referees making poor calls, just as he was prepared to cope with mistakes made by his players. “But the bunker was meant to be 100 per cent bulletproof, and it’s not,” he said. “It won’t stop here tonight. There will be more instances through the play-offs, I can promise you.” Bennett was also confused by a call in the first half to penalise Mitchell when he appeared to be struck first in an altercation with Knights centre Dane Gagai. The duel between Mitchell and Gagai was one of the highlights of the evening.

Advertisement

Newcastle coach Justin Holbrook thought “common sense prevailed” with the decision to strip Souths of the Sullivan try, while Cameron Smith said during the live commentary it did not deserve to be a try. The Knights looked like a team that was fresh from the bye the previous week, and looked in more sync in attack. Loading Souths were not helped by Walker breaking down on the half hour, with the playmaker immediately signalling to the sideline for help. He would have been unlikely to play on next weekend had Souths progressed, but Bennett confirmed the club was keen for him to play on in 2027, even though a deal was yet to be formally struck.

An early guilty plea will result in a $1800 fine, while he’ll pay $2,500 if he unsuccessfully contests it. title: ‘I wasn’t going to let him push me around’: Gagai opens up on Mitchell stoush

Newcastle veteran Dane Gagai has spoken about his personal battle against Latrell Mitchell that lit up the opening night of the finals, declaring “I wasn’t going to let him push me around.” The Knights produced a monumental upset on Friday night, beating South Sydney 20-10 at Allianz Stadium despite the absence of Jacob Saifiti, Dylan Lucas, Dylan Brown and Trey Mooney. Loading One of the highlights of the match was the running battle between Gagai and Mitchell, who last week produced the tackle of the year on Roosters playmaker Toby Rodwell at the same ground. The former Rabbitohs teammates reprised a rivalry that had stretched for over a decade at club and State of Origin level that at one point threatened to spill over on Friday night. However, Gagai was confident it would never lead to punches or a player being sent to the sin bin.

Advertisement

“Nah, it was just a heat of the moment thing,” Gagai said. “And he’s obviously sticking up for his teammate. I was trying to get the ball off Alex Johnston, and he came over, stood up for his teammate. “I wasn’t going to let him push me around. And that’s the beauty of our game. When you get competitors like that on the field – and like I said, we know what Latrell brings to a team, and he’s those players you love playing alongside – so I just needed to be that player for our team. Latrell Mitchell and Dane Gagai. Nine “And yeah, we gave each other a big hug after the game and I love the big fella, especially the things he’s doing outside of footy and in the community. But on the field, we compete.” Gagai, who will join Brisbane next year, said he didn’t go out intending to target Mitchell.

Advertisement

“I don’t think it was an individual battle within myself personally,” he said. “I was just more thinking about what can I do to help the team out. And obviously, Latrell is a big part of their team … He’s a big-game player, and he’s a superstar of the game. “But I just had to focus on my preparation throughout the week, get myself right to put myself in a position to do my job for the team, whether that’s in defence or attack. Latrell Mitchell and Dane Gagai come to blows. Getty Images “I’m always going to compete and I always look forward to the opportunity of coming up against players like that. They obviously always bring the best out of you because if you have a little micro slip, then they can punish you pretty quick. I’m just grateful that we come away with the win.” Gagai has maintained an incredible level of performance during his 16-year NRL career. The 35-year-old said he took no heed from some critics’ calls for him to end it.

Advertisement

“I don’t really listen to what other people say, and I kind of know within myself my abilities and what I’m capable of,” he said. “I guess I won’t let anyone retire me when I’m not ready. I still feel like I’m playing good footy. The body feels good. I still love the game, I still love competing. And like I said before, once I lose either the passion to play the game or the body can’t perform and keep up, then until then, I’m going to keep playing this beautiful game of rugby league and keep trying to win.” ‘He’s getting better every week’: Resurgent Rabbitoh on Walters’ World Cup radar David Fifita’s resurgence for South Sydney has earned him a place in Australia’s extended World Cup squad, while teammate Latrell Mitchell is also making a late bid for a Kangaroos jersey after sending a goalkicking SOS to a Canberra legend. An emotional Fifita this week spoke about overcoming “dark days” when injuries left him wondering if he would ever recapture his devastating early-career form.

Fifita’s barnstorming runs on the right edge, especially over the past month, have not escaped the attention of Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters, whose starting back-rowers from last year’s Ashes, Hudson Young and Angus Crichton, are injured and linking with rugby respectively. Penrith’s Liam Martin, Canterbury’s Jacob Preston, North Queensland’s Reuben Cotter, Fifita and Souths teammate Tallis Duncan have all been included in the preliminary 40-man squad all World Cup nations had to submit last Friday. Players can be added from outside the squad at a later date. David Fifita’s form has caught the attention of Kangaroos’ coach Kevin Walters. James Brickwood/SMH

“David is an elite player, and he’s put himself in the frame by getting back to the form we all know he’s capable of,” Walters said on Thursday. “He’s a big man, he likes to use his weight and power to his advantage – he loves the physical stuff. Because he’s such a big body, he needs to play regularly, which he’s been doing. He’s getting better each week, and the further Souths progress into the finals will only help him.” Souths captain Cameron Murray will be back in the green and gold should he remain fit, especially with question marks over the fitness of Panthers lock Isaah Yeo, while Mitchell is also in the frame for the end-of-season World Cup. “A person of Latrell’s calibre, the more footy he can play at this time of year, the more he’ll push his chances – we saw last week what he can do and what he brings to a team,” Walters said of Mitchell. Canberra legend Jarrod Croker spent Tuesday helping Latrell Mitchell with his goalkicking. South Sydney Rabbitohs

Advertisement

Fifita played for the Prime Minister’s XIII and Australia’s nines team in 2019, but his only Test appearances were for Tonga at the 2022 World Cup. Meanwhile, Raiders sharpshooter Jarrod Croker made the hit-and-run trip to Heffron Park on Tuesday to work with fellow left-footed kicker Mitchell. Souths’ goalkicking strike rate of 64.7 per cent (88 from 136) this season is the worst in the NRL. Improved kicking could have been the difference between fifth and sixth when you consider Cronulla finished level on competition points but 36 ahead on differential – equivalent to 18 goals. He slotted 61 from 78 (78.2 per cent) in 2022.

Croker, who lives on the Gold Coast, launched his own range of kicking tees, known as “284”, a nod to his Canberra Raiders playing number. The tees are used by Mitchell. “He reached out on the Monday, and I was at training on Tuesday,” Croker said. “The other night [against the Roosters] was his first full game back from injury, so there was a bit of fatigue, and he didn’t really have much of an exit. “An ‘exit’ is like your follow through, which gets harder when you get wider out, and only because kickers want to kick the ball harder, then stop and look up to see where it’s going. “I told him to try and keep the follow through happening, and aim it just inside the left post. The key is, ‘Aim small, miss small’, and if he’s aiming just inside that left post with his natural shape, he’ll be thereabouts most of the time.” ‘Money’s not everything’: The contract conundrum facing Panthers

Advertisement

Adrian Proszenko Penrith enforcers Moses Leota and Liam Martin have spoken of the agonising decisions they will soon be required to make on their playing careers, with the latter declaring “money’s not everything at the end of the day”. The Panthers have a raft of key stars uncontracted beyond 2027 who will be free to negotiate with rival clubs on November 1. Some of them – headlined by Nathan Cleary, Isaah Yeo, Martin, Leota and Isaiah Papali’i – have parked negotiations to focus on the upcoming finals, beginning with Sunday’s blockbuster clash against the Roosters at CommBank Stadium. Loading The club has made progress with Yeo, who was able to dedicate some time to his contract discussions while recovering from a pectoral injury, while Cleary is in no rush to make a call.

Advertisement

The club granted Leota a brief window to explore his options earlier this season, but the Kiwi international hasn’t made a decision on where he will be playing in 2028. Martin, who has been strongly linked with the PNG Chiefs, will also be in hot demand if he doesn’t recommit to Penrith before November 1. The NSW and Australian back-rower said he would “love to stay” at the Panthers, but would give his future more attention after their premiership campaign ends. “Obviously there could be more money elsewhere, but money’s not everything at the end of the day,” Martin said. “It’s also enjoying your footy. I’ve got a great bunch of mates here, like best mates, that I’ve played with since I was 18. Liam Martin has a big call to make on his future. Getty Images “And I’ve been in Penrith for 10 years now, and got a little boy. So, yeah, there’s a lot to weigh up. It’s not an easy decision, but I guess I’ll have to make it in due time.”

Advertisement

Martin and Leota have been the cornerstones of a Panthers pack that has won four premierships since 2021. They will have to balance the prospect of higher wages available elsewhere against the likelihood of joining a less successful team. “That success is so addictive, and what we’ve got here is just an incredible culture,” Martin said. “And it’s going to be very successful for a long time, this club, when you have the likes of Casey [McLean], Blaze [Talagi], Billy Phillips coming through. So, yeah, it would be hard to walk away … Related Article NRL 2026 ‘How is he doing this?’: Panthers teammates awed by skipper Yeo’s return from ruptured pec “It’s sort of the duality of it. You couldn’t imagine going somewhere and experiencing failure and just how tough that would be. But also the challenge of building a successful club somewhere else, and I feel like I could offer something. It’s a tough decision.” Leota is grappling with similar sentiments before making a call on what will likely be the last contract of his career.

“Penrith is my home and this is all I’ve ever known, so it’d be hard to sort of get me away from here. But we’ll see what happens,” Leota said. “I’m leaving it up to my manager, and if it gets done before or after [November 1] it is what it is.” The Panthers host the Roosters in a qualifying final at Commbank Stadium on Sunday. One of the highlights will be the clash between Roosters firebrand Spencer Leniu and his former teammates. Leniu almost lost his cool on several occasions in last week’s clash against the Rabbitohs, including during a running battle with Keaon Koloamatangi. “Spenny, I’m sure he would love to have his time again, and I’m sure he’ll learn from that lesson, and probably won’t be quite as fiery this week, I’m sure,” Martin said. “I’m really looking forward to the clash. title: Middle East shipping escalation about to hit every Australian wallet
text:
in brief Escalating conflict in the Middle East pushed Australian unleaded petrol prices to $2.11 per litre.

Experts warn high fuel costs will persist and could prompt further central bank rate hikes.

Australians are being warned that high fuel prices are likely to stay as the war in the Middle East reaches dangerous new levels of escalation.

As the US-led war on Iran shows no signs of ending and oil tankers are being targeted and sunk in the Strait of Hormuz by both sides, global oil prices have surged above US $100 ($139.5) a barrel.

This has led to fuel prices in Australia jumping at the bowser to an average price for regular unleaded of $2.11, a massive increase from $1.55 in July.

For diesel, oil prices increased almost 50 per cent since June.

The surging prices are sparking inflation fears and raising concerns that the Reserve Bank of Australia will lift the cash rate when the monetary policy board meets again at the end of September.

High fuel prices were the "new norm", NRMA spokesman Peter Khoury said.

"We've seen dangerous levels of escalation in the last few days, so you've got the situation where they're blowing up each other's oil tankers in the ocean, so that doesn't help."

In response to soaring prices at the start of the conflict in the Middle East in March, the Albanese government temporarily halved the fuel excise in April, slashing 26 cents off a litre.

A scaled-back extension of the fuel excise was reduced to 16 cents per litre for petrol and diesel, which lasted until 2 August.

Khoury said the government keeping its options open remained the best approach to the unfolding crisis.

"We're nowhere near where we were when we hit those record high levels.

"It is obviously expensive, more expensive than we want it to be, but it's nowhere near those levels."

Khoury urged motorists to check fuel prices in real-time and shop around for savings when filling up.

About one fifth of the world's oil transits through the Strait of Hormuz, with fighting between the two countries centring on control for the key shipping route.

title: Fixing Australia's immigration system is not just about cutting migrants
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

After the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of migrants flowing into Australia increased to "unbelievable levels", says immigration expert Abul Rizvi.

Numbers had fallen sharply during the pandemic years as lockdown measures halted international travel. By March 2021, quarterly migrant arrivals had dropped to a fifth of pre-pandemic levels in Australia.

As things returned to normal, that trend reversed.

Rizvi, a former deputy secretary at the Department of Immigration, says no one was expecting net overseas migration (NOM) — which also factors in migrant departures — to reach a record annual high of almost 550,000 people as it did in 2023.

Almost three years later, Australia is still adjusting to that influx, and politicians across the ideological divide are now fixated on setting a new figure.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The recent debate over Australia's NOM has been dominated by One Nation, which is calling for substantial cuts to immigration.

But research shows that opposition to immigration is often concentrated in areas with the fewest migrants.

Experts say these areas could also be among the worst hit by wide-ranging cuts, such as those proposed by One Nation.

Australia's temporary migration challenge

Temporary migrants have historically been a driver of population growth in Australia. Typically, more migrants arrive each year than those who leave, increasing the overall population over time.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has accused Labor of using migration to prop up headline economic numbers, saying in a media release: "Australians pay the price through lower wages, higher rents, unaffordable homes and stretched services."

To address these issues, Hanson says the number of migrants should be reduced, insisting that "international student numbers must be slashed". She has also called for the skilled migration program to be more targeted, and immigration from countries on the 'Do Not Travel' list to be halted.

The latest Department of Home Affairs figures show 2.9 million temporary visa holders were living in Australia on 31 July 2026.

New Zealand citizens can access a special temporary visa (subclass 444) that allows them to remain in Australia indefinitely. This has been available for decades but a direct pathway for citizenship was also created in 2023. Source: SBS News

The largest single group was New Zealanders holding 'special category visas', which accounted for 20 per cent (736,509) of temporary visa holders.

Temporary visa holders, who also include tourists or those undertaking short-term work or study, are not considered migrants by the ABS unless they are in the country for longer than a year.

Global migration expert and associate professor at the University of Sydney, Anna Boucher, says some temporary visa holders are still in Australia due to decisions made by former governments, including extensions granted after the pandemic by the Coalition to aid economic recovery and bridge skill shortages.

"These migration legacies can last a long time," Boucher says.

Who is considered a migrant?

To count migrant arrivals, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) looks at a person's "usual residence", using criteria such as whether they have lived in the country for 12 months or more over the 16-month period after arriving.

The latest ABS overseas migration data shows 568,400 migrants arrived in Australia in financial year 2024/25, and 262,800 left. These figures are used to calculate NOM, which was 305,600.

The ABS also releases NOM figures for calendar years. In 2024, NOM was 340,800, falling to 301,100 in 2025.

This is substantially lower than the peak in 2023, when 547,300 people entered the country, but still slightly higher than yearly figures before the pandemic.

Net overseas migration (NOM) looks at how many longer-term migrants are arriving in Australia each year. Source: SBS News

Data shows migrants on temporary visas made up 70 per cent of NOM in 2024/25.

Net overseas migration includes Australian citizens returning after living overseas for an extended period (although more Australians left in 2024/25 than returned), as well as New Zealanders, and those on temporary and permanent visas. Source: SBS News

Who are Australia's temporary migrants?

Bringing down the number of temporary migrants would involve reducing the number of temporary visas issued each year.

Hanson has said she would target international students and temporary graduate visa holders in an effort to cut NOM to 130,000. In 2024/25, students made up 43 per cent of temporary migrant arrivals.

Temporary migrants make up a large percentage of net overseas migration numbers. They include students, skilled workers and backpackers as well as 'visitors' who originally entered Australia on a tourist or other short-term visa, but extended their stay, often for work or study purposes. Source: SBS News

But Rizvi says a massive cut to student visas would have adverse effects on universities and could jeopardise the jobs of 50,000 Australians working in the international education sector.

He points out almost half of Sydney University's revenue comes from tuition fees paid by international students.

The consequences would be severe and I don't think [Hanson] has thought about those consequences.

Rizvi says it's easier to make small cuts to many visa categories than to make big cuts to one or two, as the "negative consequences become quite extreme".

But One Nation's ambitious target to bring NOM down to 130,000 would require a dramatic cut of 175,700 people per year, based on 2024/25 figures.

This could not be achieved even if all 156,700 temporary migrants on student visas each year were cut.

Labor is aiming for a more modest reduction, bringing NOM down to 225,000 within two years, according to its budget projections for 2027/28.

The Coalition says it expects NOM to be "substantially below 200,000" under its policy to cap numbers based on housing supply.

Will cuts make life better?

One reason often cited for cutting immigration is to improve housing affordability.

Boucher says reducing immigration could potentially improve rental affordability, but the impact would mostly be felt in parts of the major capital cities, particularly if cuts target international students.

Almost all students on a temporary visa live in a capital city (around 90 per cent), according to the latest Census data from 2021.

Even in the major cities, the impact on housing demand would likely be marginal, Rizvi says.

[For] people in Sydney, it would make a minimal difference in terms of their financial situation.

Boucher points out that property prices are driven by a range of factors, including the tax system and interest rate rises. Additionally, because migrant labour contributes to the construction of housing, cutting NOM could have other unintended consequences for the housing market, making the overall impact "hard to predict".

Other potential benefits, such as reduced traffic congestion, are also unlikely to be very noticeable, says Rizvi.

Four out of five temporary residents lived in a capital city, and around half lived in Sydney and Melbourne, according to the 2021 Census. Source: SBS News

On the flip side, the negative impacts of reducing NOM could include driving up prices for delivery services and food, and disruption to healthcare services.

Grattan Institute analysis of 2016 Census data found the hospitality industry had the largest share of migrant workers, with 40 per cent born overseas. Migrants made up almost half of all chefs and cooks in Australia.

It also found the healthcare and social assistance sector relies heavily on migrants, with around 37 per cent of these workers born overseas. Permanent migrants made up around one quarter of all registered nurses in the sector. They also work as aged and disabled carers, child carers and nursing support staff.

What about regional and rural areas?

Grattan's analysis found that mining areas, such as the Pilbara in remote Western Australia, are more likely to rely on migrant workers, and some agricultural areas have higher shares of working holiday makers. The sunny climate of the Gold Coast is attractive to many New Zealanders.

According to the 2021 Census, around 20 per cent of working holiday makers in Australia live in regional or rural Queensland.

Hanson, who hails from Queensland and is a senator for the state, has acknowledged the importance of seasonal workers to rural and regional communities. More specifically, she's said she wants to maintain the number of workers brought in from Pacific countries and Timor-Leste through the PALM scheme (around 30,000 workers in March 2024), even though this would likely raise NOM above One Nation's target.

But she insists this won't impact the cost of housing in rural and regional areas because these workers are often given accommodation by their employers.

"Rural and regional Australia would die if they didn't have the workers coming in, especially the abattoirs and farmers, so that's a different program," Hanson told reporters at News Corp's Bush Summit last month.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson (centre) and Nationals Leader Matt Canavan (right) at the Bush Summit in Dubbo on 27 August. Source: AAP / Pip Farquharson

One Nation and the Nationals have both criticised the Albanese government's decision to slow down the processing of working holiday visas, saying backpackers were not taking houses from people in Sydney, Melbourne or Brisbane.

But a 2021 report by Grattan, titled "Rethinking permanent skilled migration after the pandemic", noted anti-migrant views appear to be more prevalent in regional Australia, even though there are far fewer migrants there, especially from parts of Asia, the Middle East and Africa.

"This suggests a sense of threat can be as important as the level of threat," the report said.

What is the problem that needs fixing?

While simply cutting migration may not solve Australia's cost of living issues, past analysis has suggested more nuanced changes to the system could help ensure it benefits the country.

The Parkinson review of the migration system in 2023 criticised Australia's reliance on temporary migrants.

"It is not in Australia's national interest to maintain a large proportion of temporary entrants with no pathway to citizenship as it undermines our democratic resilience and social cohesion," the report said.

Experts at the Grattan Institute say it's important to get Australia's temporary intake right because most permanent visas are granted to temporary residents already in Australia.

Its report suggested allowing all migrants earning wages above a certain level to be eligible for a temporary visa, rather than restricting this to certain occupations. This would address most skills shortages, simplify sponsorship pathways for employers and limit exploitation of lower-paid workers.

It would also boost the pool of high-quality applicants for permanent residency.

Visas that offer a pathway to permanent residency should be restricted to younger workers under the age of 30, the report suggests.

It also cautioned the government against increasing the number of migrants filling low-skilled jobs in Australia, as they could "undercut the wages of low-paid Australians and further increase exploitation".

In their essay On Our Terms, former immigration policy adviser Henry Sherrell and tax researcher Lachlan Vass suggest the goal of immigration policy should be to make the lives of Australians better.

The visa system should pick people deliberately, across all parts of the system, to benefit Australians.

They say Australia needs an explicit target for migration as this would provide a clear long-term signal to state governments, employers and citizens.

The authors recommended setting net migration at 1 per cent of population growth.

"Beyond which the costs grow quickly and political support wilts [according to historical observations]," the authors note.

Australian migration is currently above 1 per cent, but the government is forecasting a rate of about 0.9 per cent in 2026/27, falling to 0.8 in 2027/28, which the authors believe is "about right".

The difficulty is getting to this figure.

Careful changes required to avoid unintended consequences

While Labor, the Coalition and One Nation have all promised to bring down NOM, no one has yet set out how this will be done, a sign of how challenging it is to balance competing interests.

"Any time you make a cut, you're going to have to upset [a particular] group," Boucher says.

Businesses want to retain skilled migrants as well as working holidaymakers who are often employed on farms; migrants want visas for family members; and those living in tourist areas also want to retain backpackers. Migrants also make a significant contribution in funding Australia's higher education sector.

Reducing immigration will impact Australia's economy because it reduces tax and visa revenue and slows population growth, which can lead to lower household consumption and reduced business profits.

A Treasury paper published in 2021 estimates that each skilled migrant provides a $198,000 benefit to the Australian economy because they generally arrive in the country after finishing their education. The average Australian costs the budget $85,000 across their lifetime because they receive more money back in services than they pay in taxes.

Skilled migrants often contribute more in taxes than they receive in services, and certain sectors such as healthcare rely heavily on overseas workers. Source: Getty / Nansan Houn

Boucher points to the UK, which is facing skills shortages in sectors like construction, healthcare, hospitality and skilled trades, after its work visas were tightened.

She says it's important Australia understands how to fill gaps if it cuts the supply of certain workers, and to be realistic about how quickly domestic workers can be trained to take their place.

A crackdown on bridging visas, which allow migrants to stay in Australia while their immigration status is being resolved, may also involve limiting or rescinding people's current legal appeal rights.

"[Cutting immigration could also] have impacts on things like human rights, like the right to reunify with family."

Where can we cut?

Although they don't agree with slashing international student numbers as Hanson has suggested, both Rizvi and Boucher believe student visas could be tightened — which Labor already appears to be doing.

One area of reform could be the 485 visa, which allows international students to live, study and work in Australia after completing their studies.

Sherrell and Vass have also suggested limiting temporary visas to a maximum of eight years, which would provide a firm deadline for people to transition to a permanent visa, or leave Australia.

Incentives could also be introduced to encourage people to leave Australia voluntarily when their visas expire. This could include allowing overstayers — those currently subject to re-entry bans — to make further visa applications from outside the country.

Superannuation taxes could also be waived, and a cash incentive of $20,000 to $30,000 paid when someone returns to their country of origin.

"This funding is comparatively cheap compared to endless weeks spent in immigration detention. And it is more compassionate too," Sherrell and Vass note.

READ MORE Cost of Nauru deportation deal revealed in late-night inquiry as PM pressed on lack of detail

Senator Jonathon Duniam, the Coalition's spokesperson for home affairs, told ABC's Insiders on 6 September that the government should find a way to deport the 77,000 illegal overstayers in Australia, and suggested temporary visa holders should be required to apply for further visas offshore.

Duniam pointed to the UK's introduction of a 'safe countries of origin' list that designates countries as generally having no serious risk of persecution and allowing for fast-track deportations.

One Nation has gone further, suggesting Australia not accept refugees from countries that the government deems unsafe for Australians to visit, citing Nepal as an example following the country’s recent devastating floods.

But cracking down on Australia's relatively low refugee intake is unlikely to shift migration numbers significantly.

READ MORE The long wait for permanency in Australia's shrinking humanitarian program

One Nation hasn't clarified whether it would reduce current humanitarian numbers from 20,000, which Prime Minister Anthony Albanese recently confirmed the government would maintain.

This is lower than Labor's previously stated target of 27,000 by 2025, but higher than the 13,750 the party was reportedly recently considering cutting it to.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor hasn't specified a number for the Coalition's refugee intake but says it will be below the former Morrison government's level of 17,875.

Boucher points out that targeting one specific group or visa class as a means of controlling migration has its limits.

If you cut [visas] in one area, how do you now that family migration is not going to spike?

She says prospective applicants will adapt to policy changes and look for workarounds; for example, a cut to student visas could trigger a spike in partner visas.

"It's in the fine grain that the decisions have to be made and that's what makes it such a challenging policy area."

title: Another major bank tips interest rates will rise before year’s end
text:
Westpac's economists finally joined their big bank peers this week, predicting the Reserve Bank of Australia is now likely to lift interest rates this year, instead of staying on hold.

Chief Economist Luci Ellis, previously an RBA Assistant Governor, says the main reasons for the shift are the growing evidence of a more resilient household sector, even as consumer sentiment tumbles, and a larger-than-expected boost to the economy from the data centre boom.

Last week’s official GDP numbers highlighted that consumers are still spending to a degree, noting the take-up of electric vehicles as a contributor. Some travellers redirected their spending locally because the war in the Middle East made it harder to leave Australia for the European summer.

Westpac joins Commonwealth Bank Australia and ANZ in pencilling in a 25 basis point increase in the official cash rate in November, while NAB thinks it’ll likely come at the next RBA meeting at the end of this month.

Inflation above the Reserve’s target of 2-to-3 per cent is also a key influence, although the next official read on consumer prices will arrive the day after the central bank’s board meeting in September.

title: Could Australia's housing downturn push the economy into recession?
text:
IN BRIEF Economists say a 10% house price fall could weigh on spending, but would be unlikely to cause a recession alone.

Retail spending and the jobs market could show whether Australia's housing slump is spreading through the economy.

Australians have watched the value of their homes soar for years. Now, as prices head in the opposite direction, there are warnings the fallout could spread well beyond the property market.

Property developer Nigel Satterley has warned Australia could face a "full-blown recession" if the housing downturn spills into consumer spending, as falling property values leave households feeling poorer and less willing to spend.

The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) has pushed back on those fears, acknowledging the downturn will slow parts of the economy but saying it does not currently expect a recession.

Which poses the question: How worried should Australians be?

Independent economist Saul Eslake agrees with the RBA that the housing downturn is likely to slow economic growth, but says falling property prices alone are unlikely to be enough to push Australia into recession.

"I don't think a decline in property prices of the orders of magnitude that people are now talking about ... that is to say, maybe of the order of 10, perhaps in some cities 15 per cent over a one or two-year period, I don't think that on its own would precipitate a recession," he said.

"It would certainly contribute at the margin to some slowing in economic growth."

AMP Chief Economist Shane Oliver also believes a recession is not the most likely outcome, but sees a greater risk that the housing downturn could contribute to one if prices continue falling and the broader economy weakens.

"Recession isn't my base case, but the risk is significant," he said, putting the probability at around 30 per cent and rising.

Why falling house prices can affect how we spend

At the heart of the concern is something economists call the "wealth effect".

Put simply, when the value of an asset such as a home rises, people can feel wealthier and become more comfortable spending. When its value falls, the opposite can happen.

Oliver said previous RBA analysis suggested a 10 per cent fall in house prices could reduce consumer spending by about 0.8 per cent after six months and 1.6 per cent over the longer term.

That matters because household consumption makes up a significant portion of economic activity.

"If the economy is weak enough to start with because of higher interest rates and other things, then that could potentially knock us into recession because the consumer is about 60 per cent of the economy," Oliver said.

But Eslake said the relationship between property values and spending was not necessarily straightforward.

For most Australians who own only the home they live in, he said its value was largely "paper wealth" unless they sold.

If someone is selling to buy another property, falling prices also mean the home they are moving into is likely to be cheaper.

"So they're not necessarily worse off in a real or tangible sense," he said.

Earlier this week, RBA assistant governor Sarah Hunter also said the impact of falling house prices on consumer spending was likely to be relatively small.

What about Australians who recently bought?

Both economists pointed to negative equity as a potentially greater concern for some recent home buyers.

Negative equity occurs when the amount someone owes on their mortgage exceeds the value of their property.

Eslake said that position only becomes a tangible loss if someone is forced to sell, for example, because of unemployment, relocation or a relationship breakdown.

Independent economist Saul Eslake says the relationship between property values and spending is not necessarily straightforward. Source: AAP / Andrew Matthews /PA /Alamy

But simply knowing they are in negative equity could also cause households to cut spending and pay down their mortgage faster.

Oliver said recent buyers were likely to be particularly sensitive to falling prices.

"If you paid $1 million a year ago [and] it's now worth $800,000, you may not feel so happy, particularly ... if your mortgage is worth more than the value of the house," he said.

Could it spiral into something worse?

Oliver told SBS News that retail and consumer spending would probably be among the first places a more serious housing downturn would become visible.

In a worst-case scenario, falling property prices could make households spend less, hurting businesses and employment.

Higher unemployment could then leave more homeowners struggling with mortgages and put further downward pressure on property prices.

"You get this downward spiral, where falling house prices lead to a loss of wealth, leads to less spending, which leads to higher unemployment, which in turn leads to further falls in house prices," Oliver said.

But neither economist believes Australia is there yet.

The latest national accounts show the economy grew 2.1 per cent over the year to the June quarter, while Eslake pointed to continued employment growth and an unemployment rate of around 4.5 per cent.

"I can understand quite a significant proportion of the population will be feeling financial difficulty, pressure or stress," he said.

"That's not the same thing as a recession, and I don't think we are on the brink of one at the moment."

What are the warning signs?

Oliver said Australians should watch whether house price declines accelerate, followed by weakening household spending, fewer job vacancies and eventually rising unemployment.

Eslake similarly nominated employment, job advertisements and business confidence as important indicators.

Both also said a recession would likely require something more than falling house prices alone.

Eslake said another two or three interest rate increases over the next six to nine months would increase the risk, while an external economic or financial shock could also push Australia closer to recession.

READ MORE Home prices fall across Australia as housing downturn takes hold

Oliver said the RBA also had the ability to change course if conditions deteriorated significantly.

"If it looks like a property downturn could drive a recession, they could quickly ... refocus from worried about inflation to worried about recession and higher unemployment," he said.

For now, Eslake believes some of the dire warnings should be treated cautiously.

"I think some of the people in property interests are talking their own book."

title: Regional Australians want cheaper flights. What’s standing in the way?
text:
Bush communities are begging for more budget airfares even as regional airline Rex warns that stiff competition in small markets is pushing the airline to the brink.

Isolated and aging populations are being let down by expensive ticket costs, Madeleine Lawler, chief executive of Regional Development Australia on the Mid North Coast of NSW, warned.

Her comments came during the latest public hearing into the state of Australia's regional aviation sector.

Flights from Coffs Harbour or Port Macquarie cost about 71 cents per kilometre, but from Ballina, where budget flights are available on Jetstar, the average is 12 cents per kilometre, Lawler told the inquiry.

"When I first moved to Coffs Harbour, I was able to get a Bonza flight for under 100 bucks, or Tiger Air was in there for a while, and I was able to get around in a really affordable way," she said.

"We are slicing demand out of our economies by not having those lower price points available in the market, and that means our tourism economies suffer as well."

But half-empty planes could not cover the costs required to run a flight, so Rex shared the burden with travellers from the bush or cancelled services, the struggling airline's network strategy general manager Warrick Lodge told the hearing.

"You end up in a situation where ... carriers are forced to charge each of those passengers more to try and cover their costs," he said.

In July 2024, Rex entered voluntary administration only to be kept afloat with a taxpayer-funded package of $40 million before being bought by American company Air T in December 2025.

Despite this, it was forced to end its Melbourne to Albury route.

Rex had already provided 40,000 seats a year to a market that only had 22,000 passengers — then Qantas added another 31,000.

The airline chose to redirect services to the Melbourne to Devonport service.

Now, no airline flies Melbourne to Albury, while Rex pulled all services to Devonport in June.

Across the business, some Rex routes barely covered operating costs, while others were forced to contribute to overheads, Lodge said.

The airline has deals in place with the Queensland and WA governments, which subsidise operations in those states.

The Royal Flying Doctor Service told the hearing that regional airlines are critical to their operations.

Adequate air travel supported early intervention and helped patients avoid emergency treatment.

"Many of these flights will be to retrieve Australians who are critically ill and need urgent medical evacuation," federation chief executive Emma Buchanan said.

title: A 16-hour flight, 100,000 fans and an upset: The NFL makes its Australian debut
text:
In brief More than 100,000 people attended the NFL's season opener in Melbourne.

Nearly half the crowd was expected to be tourists from interstate and overseas.

More than 100,000 fans from across Australia and abroad flooded the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) on Friday to watch the San Francisco 49ers thrash the Los Angeles Rams 27-7 in the NFL's first-ever regular-season game in Australia.

With the match kicking off at 10am to line up with US prime time, one Rams fan at the MCG described it as the earliest he'd ever been up for a game.

"The atmosphere, I love it, but it's kind of quiet," he told SBS News. "You know, back home it would usually be a bit crazier, with both teams going at it."

"But Melbourne is beautiful, I love it," he added.

Another fan was adding Melbourne to a list of 43 overseas stadiums he'd visited. His white jersey was embroidered with patches representing each country, with a small green patch featuring a cluster of koalas to represent Melbourne on the bottom left.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"I've been to every stadium in the world where the NFL plays," he told SBS News. "It's my first time in Australia, and I love it, everyone is so nice and inviting and helpful."

"I flew all the way in from Miami, Florida, two days ago, and I'm going home tonight. I just came to witness this amazing stadium and the great people of Melbourne."

READ MORE How an NFL match in Melbourne came to be, and its historic links

Friday's game was the first of a four-year deal between Australia and the NFL, but with no guarantee a game will be played here every year, thousands of overseas fans made the pilgrimage.

A sea of red, white, blue and yellow filled the MCG, with a sold-out crowd of 100,022 fans, including thousands of visitors from the US. Almost half of spectators were expected to be from interstate or overseas, according to the state government.

Los Angeles resident Nancy Gakere took advantage of the opportunity for a holiday, stopping over in Fiji on the way to and from Melbourne to break up what could have been a 16-hour direct flight.

She said the journey was more than worth it, especially as the 49ers, pegged as the underdogs, pulled off a surprise rout.

"Everything was just great; honestly, we couldn't have planned it any better," she told SBS News.

"When this away game happened to be in Australia, we thought, why not? And we booked the trip as soon as tickets came out in April, so we have been excited about it for a while."

When Gakere saw that the 49ers away game was set for Melbourne, she saw the opportunity for a holiday down under. Source: Supplied / Nancy Gakere

"And being 49ers fans, we were not the favourites, so we came in with low expectations, and winning was a nice surprise."

Gakere said that staying in Brunswick, in Melbourne's north, had made the trip economical.

"Other than the Uber from the airport, we have just been taking the tram in and out of the city to sight-see, trying food, the bars, walking around and exploring," she told SBS News. "And we went to the Great Ocean Road, which was our main tourism activity."

Gakere said she was a little worried about Melbourne's weather forecast, but game day was a perfect sunny day. Source: Supplied / Nancy Gakere

SBS News spoke with three 49ers fans donning vibrant red jerseys and flat caps in front of the stadium before the match.

"This is amazing," said one.

"We're just so excited; 49ers fans, we're joyous all the time. It's a gathering for us. We do it every year, we just get to do it overseas this year," another fan said.

"Thank you, Melbourne, thank you, thank you. And thank you for the hospitality," another in the trio chimed in. "I was getting on the train this morning, and I was going the wrong way, and this guy pulled me on my jacket and said, 'No, you gotta go that way! The stadium is that way!'"

"Amazing people," the third friend said. "We love the hospitality, food, coffee, oh my gosh, everything has been so amazing. The trip down under has been surreal, thank you guys, we appreciate it."

Consequences of California time for the Rams

In the weeks leading up to the event, popular discussion centred on the two California-based teams' wildly different approaches to navigating the long flight and 17-hour time zone difference to Melbourne.

To the dismay of many Australian commentators, the Rams had jetted in just the morning before, with flights booked straight out after the game.

Whether the decision to keep the Rams on California time affected the team's prowess will be debated. But reigning MVP quarterback Matthew Stafford and star off-season acquisition Myles Garrett were undoubtedly bested by their San Francisco counterparts, who arrived a week earlier to acclimatise.

"Just so proud of this team. Hey, we embraced going to Australia — 15-hour flight, we're here the whole week. It was a grind, but we did it," said 49ers tight end George Kittle.

The Rams entered this new NFL season as the clear favourites to win a Super Bowl being held at their SoFi Stadium home in Los Angeles in February, with a formidable defence bolstered by Garrett.

Los Angeles Rams tight end Colby Parkinson is tackled by San Francisco 49ers cornerback Deommodore Lenoir during the second half of the first NFL match in Melbourne. Source: AAP / Scott Barbour

But the giant crowd packing into the MCG — the seventh-biggest ever for a regular-season NFL game despite an unusual morning kickoff time to accommodate US television audiences — skewed toward San Francisco.

"I love when they [Rams] came out and they were booing. We was out here for a week. We enjoyed the city. I don't think you can fly 16 hours and be ready to play," 49ers receiver Deebo Samuel Jr. told Channel Seven.

title: Card surcharges are ending soon. But the shake-up could come at a cost
text:
In brief From 1 October, credit and debit card purchases will be free from surcharges in Australia.

Banks are expected to respond by raising annual fees and offering fewer perks.

Those irritating and often uneven percentages added to bills when you tap to pay will disappear next month, but the cost of using plastic won’t vanish, and prices are set to rise.

Eftpos, Visa, Mastercard, American Express, JCB, and UnionPay purchases will be free from card surcharges from 1 October, saving consumers an estimated $1.6 billion per year. However, because surcharges cover some merchants' banking costs, prices are expected to rise.

The removal of surcharge fees is one of three changes being rolled out by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) from next month. Interchange fees, which banks charge when they process domestic card transactions, will be capped at 0.3 per cent on each payment, down from 0.8 per cent.

Merchants typically absorb these costs, and Treasury estimates the changes will save small businesses a combined $910 million a year.

And because those fees subsidise frequent flyer and rewards points programs, banks have already started raising annual fees and offering fewer perks.

Finder personal finance specialist Taylor Blackburn told SBS news that some deals at Westpac, ANZ, HSBC, MyCard, and BOQ have either changed or are slated to change from 30 September.

Taylor Blackburn, personal finance specialist at Finder, suggests shopping around for a better deal. Source: Supplied / Finder.com

"Sign-up bonus offers have already changed at ANZ, for example, they used to do a $200 credit on your first annual fee, but they're getting rid of that," Blackburn said.

Other frequent flyer bonus offer cards have dropped by 50,000 bonus points, but some banks are improving their offers, so shop around for a better deal now before you get stung by shifting offers, he suggested.

Westpac is lifting interest rates on some of its credit cards and will increase annual fees. NAB credit card interest rates will rise 1.5 per cent too.

Commonwealth Bank announced its Commbank Awards program is changing how consumers earn points in a new loyalty and points scheme.

St George Bank is also lifting interest rates on its Amplify Qantas Platinum credit card and introducing an annual fee of $125. The bank has also dropped the interest-free period on purchases by 10 days.

New interchange caps for foreign-issued cards will start from 1 April 2027.

Australian Banking Association (ABA) chief executive Simon Birmingham said last year that interchange fees in Australia are "already among the lowest in the world".

"We agree with the RBA's concerns about fairness for small businesses, but there are better, more targeted ways to address this without destabilising the broader payments system — such as a small business interchange rate."

The European Union caps fees for debit cards at 0.2 per cent and consumer credit cards at 0.3 per cent.

In the US, rates typically range between 1.15 per cent to 3.3 per cent plus a small flat fee per transaction.

READ MORE How to slash your bills and get money back into your pocket quickly

The third RBA reform starting in October will force EFTPOS, Mastercard and Visa to publish the merchant fees they charge so businesses can compare rates and avoid paying higher-than-average fees.

Birmingham said banks are supporting their business customers to prepare for the changes.

"While the RBA estimates that only one in every six businesses choose to apply a card surcharge, it's a practice that Australians will be happy to see the back of," Birmingham said.

"From next month, the price consumers see in the aisle or on the menu will be the price they pay at the checkout. Similarly, when you shop or pay a bill online, you won't be hit with a card surcharge when you enter your payment details."

COSBOA CEO Skye Cappuccio wants more support for small businesses. Source: Supplied / COSBOA

Council of Small Business Organisations Australia (COSBOA) CEO Skye Cappuccio told SBS News hospitality and tourism businesses with tight margins that also process lots of card transactions will find the extra cost of not surcharging will add up quickly.

"Businesses that feel they have a limited ability to increase prices are highly concerned," said Cappuccio. "We would have preferred to see the interchange fee changes fully rolled out first, so small businesses knew how their payment costs would change before needing to re-cost products and services, update systems and redo business budgets.

"The priority now is making sure they have clear information from providers and that lower payment costs genuinely flow through to the businesses that need them."

title: The hidden $140 billion economy helping some Australians get ahead
text:
Key Points Three in 10 homeowners say they received family help to buy, up from about one in 10 four years ago.

From free childcare to groceries and bills, family support is reshaping what financial independence looks like.

From free childcare to home deposits, groceries and holidays, billions of dollars are flowing between Australian generations long before an inheritance is handed down.

For Shane and Catherine, being grandparents to 10 children can sometimes resemble a full-time job.

A busy week can involve seeing one or more of their grandchildren almost every day, from picking them up from school, taking them to sport, helping with homework and cooking for them.

The couple, who have both worked as educators for 45 years, made a conscious decision to become active grandparents.

Catherine even reduced her working hours so she could help care for their grandchildren while their parents worked full-time.
