"They couldn't have managed five days a week childcare. It's so expensive today," Catherine told SBS's Insight.

"So to look after the children, that's a saving in hundreds of dollars for them."

There may be no money changing hands, but the arrangement has significant financial value.

And Shane and Catherine are part of a much bigger, and often largely invisible, flow of support between Australian generations.

What is the 'Booster Economy'?

New research from SBS CulturalConnect estimates older Australians provide more than $140 billion worth of everyday financial support to younger family members each year.

The research involved in-depth interviews with 50 parents and grandparents providing support, followed by a survey of around 2,500 Australians.

More than 12 million Australians were found to support younger adult family members in some way.

Researchers have dubbed it the "Booster Economy", or the wealth and financial support flowing between generations while parents and grandparents are still alive.

And it extends far beyond the familiar "Bank of Mum and Dad" helping children into the housing market.

Among those providing support, 34 per cent had bought groceries for younger family members, 33 per cent had paid for restaurant meals and 30 per cent had bought clothes.

Almost one in five had paid for travel, while 14 per cent had bought a car and the same proportion had purchased appliances or electronics.

Forty-two per cent had provided cash, while 19 per cent had helped pay off debt.

The $140 billion estimate excludes cash transfers, debt repayments, homes and home deposits, capturing instead the scale of everyday purchases being made by older Australians for younger family members.

The Bank of Mum and Dad is getting bigger

Finder personal finance expert Sarah Megginson said its research suggests reliance on family wealth is already growing significantly in one of the biggest areas of household finances: housing.

Finder recently found 30 per cent of homeowners surveyed had received family assistance to purchase their property.

Contributions towards a deposit were the most common form of support, while 8 per cent said their family had paid for their home outright.

But Megginson said the change over time was particularly striking.

"About four years ago, those stats were looking like 10 per cent — like one in 10 were getting help from their parents," she told SBS News.

"Last year it came back around 20 per cent ... and now we're at three in 10.

"So we've just seen that trend continue to get even deeper year on year."

Megginson said older Australians were increasingly seeing the financial pressures facing their children and grandchildren and reconsidering when they passed on their wealth.

"Instead of the more traditional path of leaving an inheritance after they've gone, they've actually started, I guess, releasing it early," she said.

While housing deposits were a major example, Megginson said parents were also contributing towards expenses such as private school fees and other significant lifestyle costs.

From inheritance to everyday expenses

Megginson said the financial relationship between parents and their adult children had also changed considerably within a generation.

"I'm in my 40s, and I moved out and bought my first home in my early 20s, and that was the end of any kind of money relationship with my parents," she said.

"I was a grown-up then, paid for all of my own things."

But Megginson said younger colleagues in their 20s and 30s had described parents continuing to pay for things such as restaurant meals, or covering the cost of their children and their partners joining family holidays.

"I think that has been a huge generational shift," she said.

Housing affordability was one of the major forces behind the change, Megginson said, with the gap between incomes and property prices widening significantly over recent decades.

The report by Financial Services Council proposes changes that would see the amount of superannuation benefits left each year as a bequest halved by 2060, ensuring superannuation is primarily used up as income for retirement. Source: AAP / Moodboard

She said she increasingly heard from Australians who believed that without an inheritance or help from their parents, they would "simply never own a home".

Finder research has also found one in 10 Australians say they will need an inheritance to achieve a major financial goal, such as buying a property.

What if your parents can't afford to help?

But access to the Booster Economy is far from universal.

The SBS research highlights a stark difference between younger Australians whose families can provide significant support and those without the same financial safety net — including some who instead provide support to older relatives.

The consequences can extend beyond the immediate value of the help.

Regular free childcare, for example, can save a family hundreds of dollars a week while allowing parents to remain in the workforce. Help with groceries or bills can leave more income available for other expenses, while a home deposit can provide a pathway into a property market that might otherwise be out of reach.

Megginson said she grew up in a family that lived "pay to pay", without generational wealth to pass down.

"If you don't have generational wealth coming your way, if you're not lucky enough to be one of those 8 per cent of people who have got a house bought for them, what can you do to try and build wealth for yourself and get yourself in a better financial position?" she said.

Is financial independence changing?

Australia is also approaching a massive transfer of accumulated wealth, with previous estimates suggesting Australians aged over 60 could pass around $3.5 trillion to younger generations over two decades.

But the Booster Economy suggests some of that transfer is already happening — one grocery shop, childcare day and house deposit at a time.

Megginson believes financial pressures could even change how Australians think about independence.

While adult children remaining at home well into their 20s can sometimes be viewed as having failed to "fly the nest", she noted multigenerational living is already commonplace in many cultures.

READ MORE The taboo wealth tax debate experts say Australia can no longer ignore

"We might see a trend that is driven by finances to more embrace that style of living," she said.

"It might have some of those cultural benefits, and ... the whole 'it takes a village to raise a family' philosophy might start to flourish a little bit more."

For some Australians, that village is increasingly providing an economic safety net too — one that can look very different depending on the family you're born into.

title: Death of the auction? Sellers move to private sales in softening market
text:
in brief New data from Domain suggests more property sellers have moved away from auctions to private treaty sales.

The property platform has also found a rise in listings starting as private treaty.

Property sellers are increasingly moving away from the traditional auction in response to a softening housing market, new data from Domain suggests, with experts arguing that Australia has firmly entered a "buyer's market".

The online property platform has found a sharp rise in listings initially slated for auction being converted to private treaty in capital cities. Across Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide and Canberra, the average proportion sales that are auctions has more than doubled from 29.6 per cent in February to 60.8 per cent in July.

Listings starting as private treaty also increased at the same time, highlighting a substantial move away from reliance on auction-day results as sellers seek the best price for their asset.

Domain's chief of economics and research, Nicola Powell, told SBS News that this shift in seller behaviour reflects the softening market conditions "unravelling across the nation".

"Many sellers are testing the market and realising that there just isn't that buyer depth there anymore," she said.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

After major post-pandemic growth and following decades of steady increases, the Australian property market has seen a broad downturn over winter.

Data from property analyst Cotality shows that, while Sydney and Melbourne began to slow at the start of the year, national house price values peaked in March and have declined 3.6 per cent since.

Powell argued spring will likely be slower than usual, with Domain predicting property prices will continue to fall through the rest of the year.

"I think what we're going to see from buyers is they are going to want to get that greater value for money," she said.

The second quarter of 2026 saw the first sustained decline in national housing stock value since 2022, with Australian Bureau of Statistics figures showing a 0.3 per cent drop or $34.1 billion.

Auctions still a good idea

Shannan Whitney, co-founder of prominent Sydney property group BresicWhitney, told SBS News that shying away from auction sales could be the wrong move for sellers.

"Pricing tends to be more in line with where the market needs to be in an auction process than it does in a for sale process," he said.

"I think more vendors will be more comfortable with auction in Sydney over the next three or four months, but it just takes a little bit of time for everyone to work through the cycle."

Whitney expects the property cycle is now through its "first third" after months of price adjustments. It's "natural", he said, for sellers to want to retreat into non-auction sales where they feel safer or more in control during such a period, which he believes is now levelling off in Sydney.

"Vendors genuinely contemplating a sale are now much more aligned and educated about where the market is," he said. "Therefore, we think we expect to see clearance rates probably go up and improve over the next four months."

Sellers who aren't "in line" with the market should consider their position and perhaps pause on a sale for the next 12 months to three years, Whitney advised.

Buyers, on the other hand, are experiencing very favourable conditions. However, Whitney suggested that waiting and expecting prices to continue to drop might not be the best strategy.

Even though the market was soft, trading was better now compared with earlier in the year.

"What we're seeing now is much more engagement from buyers where they see pricing at reasonable, viable levels," he said. "We are seeing properties sell quicker now than we did six months ago."

Rapid corrections

Sustained high borrowing costs and stubborn inflation are some of the key drivers squeezing buyer affordability. At the same time, the surge in listings through autumn and winter forced national average clearance rates down to around 46 per cent.

"Listings have risen, choice is better than it once was, and particularly in markets like Sydney and Melbourne, it is very much a buyer's market," Powell said.

Economists note clearance rates below 60 per cent reduce inflationary pressure on house prices.

Major financial institutions including Commonwealth Bank have forecast a peak-to-trough decline in house prices of 8 to 10 per cent, with the market expected to hit its bottom in early 2027.

Those in the market are already pricing in the changed conditions, Whitney said, noting that the speed of information transfer at present means adjustments and property cycles happen far more quickly than they used to.

The Reserve Bank of Australia is widely expected to raise interest rates for the fourth time this year during its meeting at the end of this month. With an increased cash rate of 4.6 per cent, buyer confidence is expected to take a further hit.

If the RBA does increase rates this month, it is likely to trigger a continued "drag on inventory" as conditions slow even further.

"The cycle for buyers will lengthen and look more favourable," Whitney said.

title: 'Disfiguring': Behind the growing spread of a flesh-eating ulcer
text: In brief Buruli ulcer cases have spread beyond coastal Victoria, with new clusters reported in Melbourne suburbs. Researching are racing to find new ways to prevent the spread. Warmer weather has arrived, and mosquitoes will be buzzing about before you know it. As El Niño is expected to bring an early start to summer heat, it’s likely mosquitoes will make their presence felt earlier than usual. The threat of mosquitoes depositing flesh-eating bacteria has been restricted to a few parts of the country. But while rare, research shows it is now showing up in more areas — including in backyards in Melbourne’s inner city. So what exactly is Buruli ulcer, where is it now found, and how can you prevent it? Here’s what we know so far, and what researchers are currently developing to protect against the bacteria in future. What are Buruli ulcers? Buruli ulcer is a skin infection resulting from the bacterium Mycobacterium ulcerans. News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS. It starts as small and often painless inflammation after a mosquito bite, which may not be seen until months after initial infection. It transforms into a disfiguring ulcer after many weeks. If left untreated, it can continue increasing in size with a loss of skin and muscle. A buruli ulcer is treated with an eight-week course of antibiotics. Recovery can be much slower than expected for other common skin infections, with healing time highly dependent on the condition of the ulcer when first treated. It may take more than four months for ulcers to heal. How do people become infected? Mycobacterium ulcerans can infect urban wildlife, such as possums, which suffer symptoms similar to those in humans. Recent research has shown mosquitoes pass the bacterium to people. The mosquito most closely associated with areas at risk of Mycobacterium ulcerans is Aedes notoscriptus. Commonly known as the Australian backyard mosquito, it is widespread in Australia and commonly found in water-holding containers in suburban areas. There may be other pathways of infection, but health authorities have strongly encouraged people to prevent mosquito bites as the best way to avoid Buruli ulcer. Where is it found? Buruli ulcer has been reported in more than 30 countries around the world, including in Africa, South America and the Western Pacific. In Australia, it has been reported in several states, territories and regions, including Victoria, Far North Queensland, the Northern Territory and New South Wales. Victoria has been hit hardest, with 426 cases reported in the state in 2025 alone. Victorian cases have mostly been reported from coastal regions, but Melbourne’s suburbs have also seen an increase in activity. Inner north-west suburbs such as Essendon, Brunswick West and Moonee Ponds are part of the new cluster. With the potential for more cases, and in more locations, surveillance beyond known areas of activity is needed. Since Buruli ulcer became a notifiable disease in NSW, there have been six cases reported from the NSW south coast. There was concern this was because the Victorian outbreak had spread to the state and could also spread to new regions. But genomic analysis suggests the NSW cases are from a separate outbreak rather than spread from Victoria. This raises questions about how widespread this pathogen may be and what conditions are likely to give rise to human infections in new regions. How best to stop the flesh-eating bacteria’s spread? Australian health authorities have recommended insect repellents and reducing exposure to mosquitoes for decades to reduce the risks of mosquito-borne disease. But while health authorities might ordinarily consider insecticides to control mosquito populations, they’re not likely to be an effective way to reduce numbers of mosquitoes buzzing about the local suburbs in the long term. New research in Victoria led by two of us (Véronique Paris and Andrew Buultjens) tested a novel approach to mosquito control and found evidence that reducing mosquito numbers can also reduce a person’s risk of contracting Buruli ulcer. Using mosquitoes as pest-controllers Special devices, known as autodissemination stations, are designed to offer a breeding site to mosquitoes looking for somewhere to lay their eggs. A stinky mix of water and yeast draws them in. Once inside, the mosquito is exposed to a gauze strip coated with the control agent pyriproxyfen (an insect growth regulator) and Beauveria bassiana (insect specific fungus). When the mosquito leaves the station, its days are numbered due to the fungal infection. But before they die, they’ll transfer the mosquito control agent to other water-holding containers as they look for other places to lay their eggs. The mosquitoes become accidental pest controllers themselves. How effective was it? After eight weeks of station deployment, mosquito egg counts (a measure of mosquito activity) were 70% lower in treatment areas compared with control areas. Buruli ulcer presents an unusual challenge when trying to measure whether an intervention had impact on human disease because symptoms typically develop almost five months after infection. To account for this delay, we had to work backwards to estimate when infection likely occurred and use forensic genomic analysis to determine which cases were acquired locally. At the predicted peak of the mosquito-control effect, Buruli ulcer incidence was estimated to be 83 per cent lower in the treatment areas than in the control areas. The greater the reduction in mosquitoes, the greater the apparent protection from Buruli ulcer, providing further evidence that mosquito control can reduce disease risk. The mosquito control stations used in the study are not yet available for purchase in Australia, but regulatory approval for their use is imminent, and new products using similar approaches are also being tested. However, in this study the control stations were deployed in high numbers, so it’s unclear what the impact of their use in a single household would be. So how can you reduce your risk of Buruli ulcer this summer? Current predictions are for hot and relatively dry conditions this summer in eastern Australia. While this may mean there are fewer mosquitoes emerging from wetlands and other bodies of water, the mosquitoes closely associated with Mycobacterium ulcerans spread are found in our backyards. Water will still be available for mosquitoes around the home in bird baths, rainwater tanks, blocked drains, sump pits and roof gutters, and water left out for wildlife. To prevent mosquitoes from breeding in them, make sure you refill bird baths weekly, clear your gutters, cover water tanks, and empty and refill water for wildlife at least once per week. It’s also a good idea to keep using insect repellents. Mosquito control, whatever form it takes, will never get rid of all the mosquitoes. Covering up with long-sleeve shirts, long pants and enclosed shoes when outdoors will also help stop the bites. title: Aged care giant refunds $200,000 to residents over disputed living fees
text:
IN BRIEF Aged care provider Opal Healthcare has been forced to refund and credit almost $200,000 to its residents.

The government has introduced reforms to curb aged care providers' misuse of the Higher Everyday Living Fee.

One of Australia's largest aged care providers has been forced to refund almost $200,000 to residents after regulatory action from the Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission.

The provider, which SBS News can reveal is Opal Healthcare, refunded and credited almost 350 aged care residents following the commission's review of its Higher Everyday Living Fee (HELF) arrangements.

HELF was introduced by the Australian government in November. It is an optional fee Australians in residential aged care can pay for a higher standard of everyday lifestyle and food and beverage service.

SBS understands that the commission has found examples from a number of providers in addition to Opal for products that take advantage of the scheme.

These services, which have been reported by Australian media and have not been tied to Opal, include bundling services of Foxtel, newspapers, and wifi in a package for a resident who couldn't read, and charging residents to attend a volunteer choir that was coming to the aged care residential home.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The commission's review also forced Opal Healthcare to reform charging practices and agreements and restore or provide services it had been charging residents for, at no additional fee.

"Our regulatory and complaints work is focused on protecting residents, ensuring the standard service offer meets the requirements of residents and ensuring providers meet their obligations," commissioner Liz Hefren-Webb said.

She said providers must take "proactive steps" to ensure those impacted "receive appropriate remediation".

Opal Healthcare manages 148 residential aged care facilities across Australia, which are home to more than 13,000 residents.

A spokesperson for the aged provider said that following Opal Healthcare's introduction of the HELF program in February, there were changes to the program guidelines.

"As a result, we identified that charges to approximately 2 per cent of residents required reversal to comply with the updated guidelines. We voluntarily reversed the relevant fees for all affected residents," the spokesperson told SBS News in a statement.

The spokesperson said the service "notified the regulator" in March and "ensured the correct billing" of all residents.

In a statement to SBS News, Hefren-Webb said her office has "seen examples" of providers requiring residents to pay for services that "should already be included as part of standard residential aged care, charging for services residents cannot or do not use, or presenting optional fees as though they are mandatory".

"We expect all providers to ensure fees are charged in accordance with the rules and their obligations, and that residents understand what they are paying for," she said.

"While we won't speculate on whether further refunds may occur elsewhere, the Commission will continue to scrutinise providers' practices and take action where necessary to protect older people."

Hefren-Webb said providers with a "willingness to cooperate and undertake early remediation" would be considered when deciding disciplinary action, but this would "not prevent regulatory action where the circumstances warrant it".

“Providers that identify a problem should act immediately to prevent any further impact on residents, notify the Commission, and commence remediation without delay."

The commission's action comes as the government implement aged care reforms that would stop providers from charging residents HELF for services they'd previously received for free before November 2025.

"We've always said it was unreasonable for providers to start charging older Australians for services they previously received at no cost," Aged Care Minister Sam Rae said in a statement on Thursday.

"We've listened to older people and we are acting now to make the rules clear and strengthen protections for older Australians."

He said the government has made it "very clear" that HELF is not for services that are part of "everyday care".

"It's common sense that services a provider was already delivering continue to be provided at no additional cost."

The reform follows the package of consumer protections delivered by the government earlier this year, including the commission's power to order refunds from services that are not fulfilling their obligations.

title: Want to reduce your dementia risk? Lifestyle changes are only part of the picture
text:
IN BRIEF New research has found social and environmental dementia risk factors are largely ignored in prevention strategies.

It's estimated that by 2065, more than one million Australians will be living with dementia.

Exercise, healthy eating and blood pressure management are the most common pieces of advice for those at risk of dementia. But new research suggests Australia is ignoring crucial factors.

Dr Jennifer Dunne, an epidemiologist who was the research lead on the Curtin University paper, said dementia prevention is focused heavily "on the individual".

She said the study, published in the peer-reviewed Lancet journal, was a "broader look" at dementia risk factors, mapping them to identify where "the evidence already was".

It builds off a "large systematic review and meta-analysis" previously conducted by co-author professor Blossom Stephan, Curtin's enAble Institute Dementia chair, which identified 61 risk factors — surpassing the previously identified 14.

The research, the first of its kind, categorised the 61 risk factors using a socioecological model.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

It found a lack of knowledge on how social and environmental conditions affect dementia — information crucial for dementia prevention.

Dunne, a Curtin University Dementia Centre of Excellence research fellow, said the report identifies "gaps" where researchers "should be looking".

"There's so much focus on preventing dementia, but we need to think more broadly about how we work together to prevent it," Dunne said.

"We need to move away from the message of telling people you need to do all these [lifestyle] things because they can only be successful if the environment around them is supportive."

Risk factors are 'all interlinked'

Dementia is an umbrella term for more than 100 conditions — the most common being vascular dementia and Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's accounts for up to 80 per cent of dementia cases, and impacts a person's memory, thinking and behaviour.

Source: SBS News

Dementia is caused by neurodegeneration — damage or death of the brain's neurons.

Uncorrected vision or hearing loss, social isolation and early childhood education are among the study's 61 risk factors.

"You start thinking about dementia prevention in mid-life ... but you can't go back and do your childhood education again — you can't change that risk factor," Dunne explained.

"We need to ensure that the broader society in which we live supports high-quality education that is accessible to everybody."

She noted that employed adults face a higher risk of social isolation as they approach retirement age.

Social isolation is enmeshed with other risk factors including loss of vision, loss of hearing, physical inactivity and depression.

"We know that when people sometimes become socially isolated, they become depressed. Then they tend to withdraw and stop exercising. They might start smoking, or start smoking more, which leads to a cascade of health conditions. It's all interlinked," Dunne said.

Stephan said the research must be turned into "action".

"Dementia prevention should support healthy choices while also improving education, neighbourhoods, healthcare access and other social conditions that shape brain health across the population throughout a person's life," she said.

Dementia 'close' to a public health crisis

According to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 439,000 Australians were living with dementia in 2025 — of those, 56 per cent are women.

A person's risk of dementia increases with age, with 42.7 per cent of Australians aged 90 and over living with the condition.

Currently, dementia is the leading cause of death in Australia.

It's estimated that more than one million Australians will have dementia by 2065.

Dunne said dementia is "already pretty close" to being a national public health crisis.

READ MORE Leader in dementia research shares four ways you can reduce your risk

One way to counter that is ensuring Australians are ageing well.

"The whole goal is to keep people healthy and make sure we live in environments that are supportive to us — and that the government have a lot they can do to prevent dementia," Dunne said.

Professor Tanya Buchanan, Dementia Australia CEO, said the research reaffirmed that "dementia risk reduction is a collective responsibility".

"It is vital everyone has access to the supports and services they need to support their brain health,” she said.

“Alongside addressing brain health behaviour at an individual level, we need policies and actions from governments and organisations to make it easier for everyone to lower their risk of dementia.”

title: Donald Trump's 'only condition' for $5,000 payments to every American
text:
In brief US President Donald Trump has promised to pay every American adult US$5,000 should Republicans win the midterms.

The promise came during a lengthy speech to supporters at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Texas.

President Donald Trump said on Thursday he would pay every US adult a US$5,000 ($6,926) "Trump dividend" if Republicans retain control of Congress in November's midterm election, an extraordinary attempt to persuade voters to back his party.

"If the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000. It will be called the Trump dividend," he told the Republican midterm convention audience in Dallas, Texas.

Trump likened the payments to a corporation's distributions to shareholders, citing "our tremendous strength and success economically".

He did not say where the money would come from — with the theoretical bill likely topping US$1.35 trillion ($1.85 trillion) — citing only that "our country is making so much money".

It was also unclear how the payments would work or whether they would be legal.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The promise would require congressional approval, and would further exacerbate the country’s nearly US$1.8 trillion annual budget deficit and concerns about inflation.

The payment would also come with a catch — Trump was clear he only wanted US citizens spending their prospective windfalls at home.

"But the only condition on the payment of this dividend that we’re going to be making … is that it must be spent in the United States of America," Trump told the convention crowd.

"We don’t want you going to Canada to spend the money. We don't want you going to China, to Germany. We got to spend the money in the United States of America."

Trump did not say how he and his administration would ensure the funds were only spent in the US.

During a primetime address that lasted an hour and 45 minutes, Trump boasted of completing "the greatest two years in the history of the presidency", putting himself squarely at the centre of the election despite his deepening unpopularity.

But it was not clear whether his campaign-style speech would appeal to the critical swing voters who opinion polls show have drifted away from Trump's party, amid growing dissatisfaction with the cost of living and the war on Iran.

"We hand America's future to the radical left Democrats, and our nation will spend the next decade just getting back on its feet," he said. "Vote Republicans, and we will leave the world in our dust for generations to come."

Within an hour, vice president JD Vance appeared to try to walk back Trump’s proposal — at least in part — by suggesting the dividend payments would not go to the wealthy. Vance suggested it could be paid for by US tariff revenues, though the suggested payment dwarfs what the US has taken in through the protectionist measures.

The US Congress would need to approve or otherwise acquiesce to the payment. The sum would far exceed US tariff revenues even before the Supreme Court tossed much of the president’s tariff program last year.

The national debt last month topped US$40 trillion ($55 million) for the first time.

Trump has frequently lamented that, during the modern era, the sitting president's party almost always loses seats in Congress during the midterms, and he has looked for unorthodox ways to defy the trend, including this week's convention.

"We’re going to change that,” Trump said. “There’s no reason for it."

New Mexico-based lawyer John Day said Trump's proposal would have to be approved by Congress, but it would be legal because the payment would go to everyone regardless of how they voted, or whether they voted at all.

"This is a campaign promise," Day said. "It’s not a payment to individuals to try to get them to vote in a particular way."

In search of a 'Trumpapalooza' poll bump

The two-day Dallas gathering, where Trump will also deliver the closing remarks on Friday after Vance's keynote address, underscores the extent to which Republicans' fortunes are tethered to Trump and serves as a showcase for their strategy ahead of the 3 November midterm elections.

The event was so centred on Trump that Republican National Committee chairman Joe Gruters informally dubbed it "Trumpapalooza," a nod to the popular Lollapalooza music festival.

The focus on Trump amounts to a risky bet that he can mobilise the voters who carried him to the presidency two years ago, despite public polls showing his approval ratings have hit an all-time low. Trump vowed to pay multiple visits to battleground states and districts in the eight weeks until election day.

"I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot," Trump said, a line that may have pleased Democratic campaign strategists just as much as MAGA voters.

title: The ‘unique’ Docker standing between the Swans and another grand final
text:
Advertisement

Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 The ‘unique’ Docker standing between the Swans and another grand final Jonathan Drennan September 12, 2026 — 1:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After completing an intense week of training on Friday afternoon, Swans players were divided on what to do that evening. Some wanted to watch the semi-final between Fremantle and Geelong, which would determine their opponent in next weekend’s preliminary final. Others were happy to tune out of footy for the night and wait until they reconvened to begin the forensic analysis of their next match. The Swans who did tune in to the Dockers’ tense 14-point victory at Optus Stadium were treated to an exceptional performance from ruckman Luke Jackson, with the onus now shifting to how to stop him at the SCG. Loading Swans coach Dean Cox, one of the AFL’s greatest ever ruckmen, will be aware that if Sydney can nullify Jackson, another grand final is possible. Jackson was a key man in Fremantle’s minor premiership, but the Dockers are by no means a one-man band. Jackson was joined on this year’s All-Australian team by four teammates: Shai Bolton, Jordan Clark, Murphy Reid and Josh Treacy. Against the Cats, Bolton was outstanding, kicking two goals and finishing with 26 disposals. But it was Jackson who flipped the game.

Advertisement

With five minutes left of the third quarter, Fremantle had conceded three successive goals and their home crowd was tense. Jackson, a former Australian under-17 basketball star, finished the quarter with eight disposals, two goals, four score involvements and 12 hitouts. In their previous meeting this season, in Perth in July, the Swans held a two-point lead at the end of the third quarter before Fremantle kicked nine goals in the final term to win by 38 points and underline their premiership credentials. Luke “the Unicorn” Jackson was nothing short of brilliant for the Dockers. AFL Photos In that game, Swans ruckman Brodie Grundy had 29 hitouts to Jackson’s 26, with Fremantle also able to utilise Mason Cox, who had 10 hitouts. The Swans do not have a deputy with the experience of Cox, having recently used forward Hayden McLean to relieve the veteran Grundy at stoppages. Grundy’s dominance has been a foundation of Sydney’s finals run, but against Jackson in the preliminary final he will face one of the biggest tests of his career. Grundy cannot match Jackson’s scoring threat, with the Fremantle ruck averaging a goal a game and finishing the season with 27 majors, a rarity for his position.

Advertisement

But in the core skill of hitouts, Grundy averages 34.3 a game compared to Jackson’s 25.7. Grundy also possesses an ability to act as an auxiliary midfielder when needed and will need to do so to curb Jackson’s influence. The Swans’ midfield trio of James Rowbottom, Jai Serong and Errol Gulden combined beautifully in their qualifying win against Brisbane to help dominate clearances, but a lot of their success came through Grundy’s dominance at stoppages. Brodie Grundy tussles with Luke Jackson in the last meeting between the sides, in Perth in July. AFL Photos via Getty Images Grundy’s presence in the Swans side has transformed their ability to score from clearances. According to Champion Data, no player has averaged more hitouts-to-advantage at centre bounces than Grundy (3.9) since 2024. This season, the Swans rank No.1 for scores from clearance, and they have 14 wins and 0 losses when they outscore the opposition from clearance, highlighting the importance of Grundy’s ability to outwork Jackson.

Advertisement

Fremantle will travel to face a heavily depleted Swans team missing the suspended Riley Bice, Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Nick Blakey. Captain Callum Mills is also missing from the backline after suffering an ACL injury against Brisbane, depriving them of vital on-field leadership. Related Article Sydney Swans ‘You just have a lot more to lose’: How fatherhood has centred Swans star Grundy History is not on Fremantle’s side at the SCG. Fremantle have won six times at the stadium and lost 14 times. However, more recently, Fremantle have won two out the last three games at the SCG dating back to 2023. The AFL will on Sunday confirm the date and time of the preliminary final. In his post-match press conference on Friday, Geelong coach Chris Scott was full of praise for the impact of Jackson. “I always hesitate to say unique, but he’s as close as there is to unique in that position as there is in the competition,” Scott said. The Swans also have their own unique ruckman. The contest between them will go a long way to deciding which side progresses to the grand final.

title: Jiu-jitsu coach, stand-up comic, apiarist: Inside the surprise day jobs of Sydney’s councillors

For 40 years, Victor Macri has spent five days a week cutting hair at Fernando’s Hair, the business his father started in Marrickville in 1960. A dispute with local councillors over a building matter prompted Macri to run as an independent for the former Marrickville Council – which was later merged to form the Inner West Council – in 2004. Victor Macri has been a part of the Marrickville community for four decades. Sam Mooy But the veteran councillor still spends Tuesday through Saturday giving haircuts with an ear to the ground. “That’s how I keep in contact with the community,” Macri says. “I get all the complaints.” He is among hundreds of local councillors in NSW for whom public office is not their primary source of income. From retail workers and Uber Eats drivers to martial arts masters and cosmetic surgeons, Sydney’s council chambers are filled with elected officials juggling a range of jobs.

Advertisement

Mayors and councillors at the state’s 128 local councils are not paid full-time wages but receive fees determined by the Local Government Remuneration Tribunal. Those payments are determined by the size and type of council on which they serve. For example, a City of Sydney councillor is paid between $32,810 and $48,140. In Strathfield, it’s between $10,920 and $24,080. Northern Beaches councillor Jody Williams is a trade lane gatekeeper three days a week at Bunnings, where he loads cars and checks receipts – and the community’s pulse. Northern Beaches councillor Jody Williams keeps an eye on the local economy by working at Bunnings. Janie Barrett He replies to emails during his lunch breaks, and Saturdays through Tuesdays are booked with council commitments, community events, and citizenship ceremonies. Williams, a member of the Your Northern Beaches Independent Team, estimates he spends about two hours everyday reading council documents, but says it’s worthwhile. “When you’re of service to other people, you forget about your own problems ... It’s about dopamine, and doing nice things for people,” he says.

Advertisement

Lane Cove Labor councillor David Roenfeldt drives buses from Sydney Airport to Yass and Canberra, while Bayside Council’s Chris Saravinovski, also Labor, works as an airport ramp agent, and is a jack-of-all-trades from baggage handling to health and safety. Saravinovski says council work is flexible and rewarding. Related Article Sydney councils This Sydney council was meant to pick a new deputy mayor. A jaunt to the UK got in the way “It’s not for the money,” he says. “You can’t survive on it ... I don’t blame any other councillor having another job and picking this up as a side thing.” Wollondilly Mayor Matt Gould, an independent, once juggled council with drone piloting. Since becoming mayor, he resolved he could do “both poorly or one properly”. Bayside Liberal councillor Dr Ron Bezic is a cosmetic surgeon, while the Hills Shire’s Dr Mila Kasby is a Greens councillor who stepped away from her veterinary practice to focus on volunteer work. She says the system favours financially comfortable candidates. “We need a whole range of different people from different backgrounds … because councillors aren’t paid a living wage, I think that excludes a lot of people,” Kasby said.

Advertisement

Hawkesbury councillor Shane Djuric, who is a Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party member, was a beekeeper, but retired following a 2023 injury. Trade-offs between full-time work and council push some to rely on side hustles. Katie Little once spent her spare time on the DJ circuit. Now, she picks up odd jobs like dog boarding. James Brickwood Lane Cove Labor councillor Katie Little, a former DJ and stand-up comedian, manages a retirement village, but also boards dogs at her home. Striking the balance between single motherhood, having a day job, and being a councillor made side hustles necessary. “When I started dog boarding, the dogs sent to me came with food better than my kids and I were surviving on,” Little says. Ethan Hrnjak, a Greens councillor from the Northern Beaches, studies law at Macquarie University. His odd jobs have included test kitchen assistant at KFC headquarters, and Uber Eats driving.

Ryde’s Felix Lo is a notary public and a Brazilian jiu-jitsu coach taking up to 15 classes a week. The Labor councillor says the similarities between governance and BJJ run deeper than it might seem. “Jiu-jitsu is very much physical, but it’s also like playing chess. Every move, you have to be very careful ... This analogy can apply to local politics and in running the city, right?” Dr Felix Lo studied law at university and teaches regular jiu-jitsu classes. Wolter Peeters Blacktown has a retired NSW police chief inspector, Robert Fitzgerald, a Labor councillor, and police prosecutor Mohit Kumar, a Liberal, on council. Kumar, who spends his days at Blacktown Court House, says his capacity is constrained by the fact his council role isn’t full-time. “There are a lot of sacrifices you got to make, especially with family.” Some professions feature repeatedly. title: Dust-up over new quarry divides coastal town that’s become a hit with tourists
text:
Advertisement

NationalVictoriaMining Dust-up over new quarry divides coastal town that’s become a hit with tourists Benjamin Preiss September 12, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Atop the rolling hills of Fish Creek, the panoramic South Gippsland coast stretches out below in stunning glory. The Strzelecki Ranges, Wilsons Promontory, Corner and Shallow inlets are among the world-class landscapes that greet both travellers and locals alike. For more than 30 years, this treasured landscape has drawn in residents and small-scale farmers who have built homes and livelihoods within Fish Creek’s lush green hills. Plans for a new quarry, nearby an existing pit, have sparked concerns among residents in Fish Creek. Eddie Jim But soon, the view may also include a gaping hole in the ground, with plans to build a new quarry among the idyllic farmland triggering alarm in the community amid concerns about dust, noise and environmental damage. But the operator, which runs an existing mudstone quarry on the same parcel of farmland, insists it is aiming to address legitimate concerns through good design and appropriate operating controls.

Advertisement

Fish Creek Quarries says it is planning to begin constructing a new quarry near its existing pit, which is reaching the end of its life. The current quarry produces primarily mudstone and shale rock, which is typically used for farm tracks, laneways and access roads. Richard Gange is among the residents who fear the proposed quarry will be harmful to the environment and their health. Having bought his property, which neighbours the quarry, about 30 years ago, Gange has raised his three daughters there together with his wife. “It’s catastrophic for us,” he said of the proposed quarry works, which will be metres from his house.

Advertisement

Gange said he has watched the existing quarry grow from a small operation several decades ago into a large worksite with frequent truck movements. While tree planting and the deep level of the existing quarry helped mitigate some dust and noise over the years, he said the new plans ignited fears locally about exposure to crystalline silica dust, which can result in the lung disease silicosis. Land surrounding the quarry had also been subdivided, he said, which had brought a higher population density to the area and made resource extraction no longer appropriate in the Fish Creek hills. Richard Gange and his wife Sita Morton at the Fish Creek property overlooking Wilsons Promontory. Eddie Jim “This is not a small quarry,” he said. “The town has changed. We’re a tourist destination now.” Oil producer and Golden Creek Olives co-owner Rima O’Sullivan said the new quarry would loom over her farm, which is home to about 1000 olive trees, and she fears dust from the proposed resource extraction could contaminate her oil production process.

Advertisement

“It’s windy here,” she said. “There’s no doubt the dust is going to blow off that hill.” O’Sullivan said the quarry currently produced little noise because it was surrounded by trees and workers were quarrying deep beneath the surface, but the new proposed site would decapitate a large hill and kick up dust plumes. Rima O’Sullivan at her olive farm. Eddie Jim “We’re not anti-quarry,” O’Sullivan said. “It’s just too close to housing and businesses.” The proposed extraction site is 17.3 hectares within a broader work authority area of almost 50 hectares.

Advertisement

Fish Creek Quarries spokeswoman Emma Hicken said the company intended to finish operations in the current pit and then move into the new extraction site. “This will allow us to continue supplying an important local source of mudstone and shale, while also allowing us to progressively rehabilitate the existing pit,” she said. A view of the proposed quarry site with a vineyard below. Eddie Jim Hicken said the early stages of proposed pit would be positioned so it was largely hidden within the surrounding landscape. However, the new quarry will be significantly bigger than the existing pit if it proceeds. Friends of the Earth’s Strzelecki Koala Collective has also lashed plans for the new quarry, arguing the farmland earmarked for the extraction site provided a “highway” for native wildlife to the nearby Hoddle Range Flora Conservation Reserve.

Advertisement

Hicken said concerns about koalas should not be dismissed, but said the proposed pit had been designed without removal of native vegetation. She said further planting could create additional habitat. However, an existing windbreak consisting of trees planted by the quarry property owner would need to be removed as part of the proposal. Related Article Victorian election ‘We are not banjo-playing dimwits’: The deep rural resentment that will shape the election Hicken also acknowledged the presence of crystalline silica in the quarry materials, but said the company was working with environmental and regulatory authorities to minimise dust impacts. “Our focus is on preventing dust where we can, controlling it at the source and making sure the right monitoring and management measures are in place.” South Gippsland Shire chief executive Allison Jones said the council had not received any planning permit applications for the site. Before the quarry operator can lodge an application with the council, it must first obtain the required licences from the state government.

Advertisement

Resources Victoria said it had not yet received an application for a new quarry at Fish Creek. However, a spokesman for the agency said it had approved 10 new quarry licences, known as work authorities, during the 2025-26 financial year. Kim Kemper is among the residents worried about the new quarry in Fish Creek. Eddie Jim Kim Kemper is among the locals struggling with the stress of uncertainty about exactly when or if the new quarry will proceed. The proposed work authority is about 20 metres from her property’s boundary, and about 50 metres from her house. Kemper said it was impossible to plan for the future with the prospect of a massive quarry next door. “We’re in limbo,” she said. “I hate it.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. title: The Roosters’ wheels came off at exactly the wrong time. Can they go back to the future?
text:
Advertisement

Analysis SportNRLNRL 2026 The Roosters’ wheels came off at exactly the wrong time. Can they go back to the future? Dan Walsh September 12, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In the “before time” of four weeks ago, when Sam Walker still roamed the field without a moon boot, the Roosters were premiership favourites. As James Tedesco notes, you don’t exactly forget “the best defensive performance of your season”. Loading The Tricolours’ stirring 12-6 upset of Penrith on August 13 wasn’t just their most recent victory. It was the club’s biggest win in years, finally shaking the chokehold Ivan and Nathan Cleary had held them in – to the tune of an 11-1 record – in the six-again era. They rattled Nathan like never before, regularly rushing up on the champion No.7 given Isaah Yeo was sidelined, shutting down Penrith’s attack with goal line defence (occasionally illegal) that harked back to their halcyon 2018-19 premiership-winning days.

Advertisement

Ten days later, the Roosters lost to the Tigers. They’re still yet to fully recover. Walker went down the following week against the Dolphins, and Trent Robinson chose to cut his losses and rest nine of his best players for the local derby against the Rabbitohs, which they lost by 30. That Panthers breakthrough capped an eight-game winning run, in which they conceded a miserly 12.8 points a game (the best record of any side over that period). The rhythm that went out the window in a bludging Sunday afternoon, 25-24 loss to the Tigers briefly returned against the Dolphins a week later.

Advertisement

But both losses were set up by alarming defensive lapses – the kind Penrith have taken and beaten teams senseless with for years now. The Roosters coughed up three tries between the 19th and 26th minutes to the Tigers – two down their right edge and another directly from a fumbled pass on their own line. The Roosters were premiership favourites just a month ago. NRL Imagery The Dolphins peeled off three tries in nine minutes before half-time, targeting Daly Cherry-Evans and Rob Toia’s suspect decision-making on the Roosters’ left. “When things don’t go our way, we’ve struggled to get back to what we do well,” Tedesco says – having been sidelined (and rested) for all bar the Dolphins game in the past month.

Advertisement

“We can’t let things snowball, and in those games, one bad thing has led to another. So I think that’s on me as captain and the leaders to help fix that up against Penrith. Things aren’t always going to go perfectly. But you can’t let that slide for 15-20 minutes either. You have to move onto the next job and recover.” How the Roosters’ attack recovers without the enigmatic Walker and adjusts to the probable scrum-base combination of Daly Cherry-Evans and Hugo Savala is key. “Maybe they become a little more structured,” champion playmaker and ex-Roosters halves coach Cooper Cronk says. “Maybe they [adopt] a little bit more of a set-play mentality – play one, two, three [settling plays] and then play off the back of that.

Advertisement

“Sam Walker’s effectiveness is his unpredictability. Maybe the Roosters narrow that down a bit and start doing a little bit of sequence play to get the best out of Savala and Cherry-Evans.” The returns of Victor Radley (concussion), Daniel Tupou (back last week from a lengthy shoulder injury) and Angus Crichton (broken foot) can’t be overstated. Can Daly Cherry-Evans get the Roosters’ campaign back on track? James Brickwood The Roosters attack was the definition of clunky against the Tigers. Without Radley holding them together in the middle, and then understandably when rocked by Walker’s injury, they were listless for much of the Dolphins clash too. For all their attacking wares, the Roosters haven’t been that flash attacking from inside the opposition’s 20-metre zone all season.

Advertisement

But the 43 tackles they had pressing the Tigers’ line, and 38 doing the same from inside the Dolphins’ 20, should have been enough to win both matches by their standards. The Roosters have still scored the most tries from kicks (33) of any team this season. But of late, one of their best attacking weapons has been holstered – Rex Bassingthwaighte’s 79th-minute try against the Rabbitohs last week was their first from the boot in a month. Recent form, pundits, punters and the bookies alike give the Bondi-based side little hope against the Panthers. The Penrith juggernaut does seem to be rolling once more, with Yeo back in the middle and Cleary as imperious as ever. But Robinson and the Roosters have been here before – losing back-to-back games late in their 2013 and 2018 premiership runs, with a 2013 upset loss to the Gold Coast especially memorable given the Titans were $12 outsiders at kick-off.

Advertisement

And even without main man Walker, the Roosters still boast an array of talent and firepower that most NRL rivals could only dream of. And they know it. “We know we’ve got the X-factor to compete with anyone,” Tedesco says. “And especially against Penrith, you can’t hold back or play too safe. But we have to be ready to do the tough things first, and that starts with our defence and our kick-chase – doing those little things right will earn us the chance to play our style of footy and then put some pressure on them.”

title: ‘One tough kid’: Boy, 15, found after days clinging to capsized boat in frigid water off Alaska
text:
Advertisement

WorldNorth AmericaAlaska ‘One tough kid’: Boy, 15, found after days clinging to capsized boat in frigid water off Alaska John Seewer September 12, 2026 — 1:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Toledo, Ohio: A 15-year-old boy survived on top of an overturned skiff in Alaska’s frigid Bering Sea for about two days, losing his older brother and then his cousin to the ocean after the boat capsized while they were out fishing. The teen, identified by a relative as Derek Parker Aghnaanga, was finally hoisted to safety by a fishing boat near St Lawrence Island – a remote Alaskan island closer to Russia than it is to the United States. The bodies of his cousin and brother were also recovered. Loading The cousin had held on to the overturned boat for a while too, but did not survive to be rescued, the teen told one of the rescuers. The captain of the fishing boat that came to his aid said Aghnaanga clung to the skiff through darkness and water temperatures about 10 degrees Celsius.

Advertisement

“That’s one tough kid,” Adam White, captain of The Northwest Explorer, told KTUU-TV in Anchorage. “Through teeth chattering, he had mentioned that his brother was still under the skiff,” White said. “And then he said that, in the previous night, before our rescue, that his cousin had slipped away.” Derek Parker Aghnaanga, 15,was pulled to safety from the overturned hull of his skiff by the crew of a fishing vessel. Rob Suryan/NYT US Coast Guard planes and helicopters spotted the skiff on Monday after family members reported the three missing the night before. The group left the village of Savoonga on St Lawrence Island last Friday and planned to return early Sunday, the Coast Guard said. Halibut fishing is a part of the culture and important to survival in the village where there are about 800 residents and jobs are hard to come by, said Collen Walker, an aunt of the brothers. Residents often share their catch with family and neighbours, she said.

Advertisement

“That’s how we do it in our community. We take care of one another,” she said. “We still live a traditional way of life even if the world is changing.” Aghnaanga, the teen rescued, often went fishing with his 35-year-old brother, Sidney Kulowiyi, and looked to him as a father figure ever since their own father died when they were younger, Walker said. A fishing boat came to the stranded teen’s aid after he was spotted. Carlos Alexis Escartin via AP She described Kulowiyi, a commercial fishing captain, as a humble and loving “provider for people in the village”. She didn’t want to release the name of their cousin who died, saying he also came from Savoonga. Their skiff capsized Saturday night far out in the ocean, she was told.

Advertisement

The Coast Guard said one of its aircrews spotted the boy Monday morning and deployed a raft and supplies before contacting The Northwest Explorer. Aghnaanga’s mother was listening to a radio transmission of the rescue on Monday while other family members huddled around a speakerphone, Walker said. “We all cried and jumped for joy when the captain announced on the radio, ‘We found a kid, he’s alive, he’s alive,’” she said. “Then we asked, ‘Where’s the rest of them?’” Video of the rescue shows Aghnaanga in a bright yellow jacket kneeling atop the overturned skiff. The boat’s crew tosses him a line, tugging the skiff closer until they can pull him into a rescue basket.

Advertisement

He was experiencing symptoms of hypothermia when he got onto the boat, the Coast Guard said. The fishing boat crew warmed him with blankets and hot packs, its captain said. The Queensland government’s wage bill is set to jump a further $93 million this financial year, after the industrial umpire ordered a 4.75 per cent lift to award rates and allowances. The Queensland Industrial Relations Commission decision on the 2026 State Wage Case, published late on Friday, ultimately mirrored its federal counterpart’s July call. Unions had sought the 4.75 per cent rise, which the state conceded would be hard to “argue strongly” against despite warning of the pressure such a rise would put on its $40 billion wages bill. The increase will apply to some specific awards, but will also flow wider into the public sector, including to some workers who were unlikely to have otherwise seen a pay rise this year. Matt Dennien The decision also follows Queensland’s first credit rating downgrade in almost two decades over “weaker budgetary performance”, putting even more pressure on the Crisafulli government.

Advertisement

The 4.75 per cent lift will apply to awards largely used for staff of First Nations councils, Parents and Citizens Associations, and auxiliary firefighters, but will also flow wider into the public sector. This is because a range of collective agreements between much of the sector and the state include clauses to ensure their wages are not below those set in the relevant award. The state ultimately put its position that given the prevailing economic conditions, the industrial context, and all the information before the Full Bench, it would be a difficult task for the state to “argue strongly” against a 4.75% increase. QIRC 2026 State Wage Case decision In documents filed as part of the case, Treasury put this figure at up to 29 of the state’s collective agreements – including six that are in arbitration – with a total cost of $93 million across 2026-27. title: From ‘faster, higher stronger’ to ‘bolder, shorter, louder’ – athletics takes a great leap
text:
Advertisement

SportAthleticsOlympics Opinion From ‘faster, higher stronger’ to ‘bolder, shorter, louder’ – athletics takes a great leap Michael Gleeson Sports columnist September 12, 2026 — 12:15pm

September 12, 2026 — 12:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The black cat analogy wittily describes the differences between religion and science. Philosophy, thus, is like being in a dark room looking for a black cat. Metaphysics is being in a dark room looking for a black cat that isn’t there, while theology is being in a dark room looking for a black cat that isn’t there and shouting, “I’ve found it”. Usain Bolt has lent his star power to World Athletics Ultimate Championships. Getty Images Sport, as a modern religion, has this week joined the analogous spectrum, coming in after metaphysicians. Sports administrators are blind people in a dark room looking for a black cat that might or might not be there but figure if they make themselves smaller and use TikTok the cat will come to them. This week against the backdrop of the NFL – America’s biggest, brashest sport – liberating a new foreign land, other sports were wondering how they got bigger, brasher and brassier? But mainly bigger. It can’t be all Tay Tay and Travis Kelce.

Advertisement

New national tennis honcho Andrew Abdo floated the idea of cutting early matches at the Australian Open back to three sets, an idea quickly put back in the bottle by Tennis Australia. Abdo is a former NRL guy. The organisation he now leads runs the Australian Open, which these days has so many people queuing to get in they’ve stretched it out over even more days. Abdo wouldn’t be the first administrator to suggest more event, less sport. New AFL chairman Craig Drummond has leafed through the same sport marketing playbook. Footy with a new Tassie team coming in will mean a longer season. They could have a shorter one (as if) and play each other once. That would satisfy integrity concerns over a compromised fixture. But they won’t do that. They’ll schedule more games but make them shorter. The NFL brought its unrivalled pizazz to the MCG on Friday. Getty Then Cricket Australia this week decided its shortest version T20, introduced as the panacea for Test cricket’s shortcomings, or longcomings as it turns out, was so good they would invite private owners to spend their millions on Big Bash League teams. England cricket, meanwhile, had previously decided that making cricket shorter was such an effective ploy they would double down and make it shorter still. They introduced The Hundred. It goes for 100 balls. If they could distil it to an over and run it as an ad break they might. T20 was soooo long and boring. This in a country where Great Rail Journeys vies with Midsomer Murders for entertainment.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 The NRL is a one-man band. The AFL is not. Both codes are open to a rebellion Roy Masters Sports Columnist Which brings us to this weekend in Hungary. Athletics, a sport that has to scream to be heard outside of the Olympics every four years and, at a pinch, during the bi-annual World Championships, has sallied forth into this brave new world of reinvention. On Friday in Budapest, the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship was launched. It’s a title that sounds like it’s aimed at the professional wrestling market. The event is a drastically cut-back, invitation-only all-stars version of the World Championships. Essentially, it’s an abridged major competition to fill a hole in the calendar in the off-years when there are no World Championships. But it looks nothing like a regular championship.

Advertisement

Firstly, it goes for three night sessions of three hours each, instead of nine days of morning and night sessions. So that means a heap of events miss out, some mercifully so, but each night has at least one throwing event and one jumping. There are no heats and fewer rounds. There are 28 finals, with straight finals held in all field events as well as the 800m, 1500m and the 5000m. The shorter distance races will have no heats and only two semi-finals. Sprinter Noah Lyles has backed the Ultimate Championships but isn’t fit enough to compete. Getty Images “The Ultimate will not follow a conventional timetable but rather a show script in which every second is accounted for. Scenario-planning between broadcast and event presentation ensures that moments of surprise and delight are captured and that no storyline will be missed,” World Athletics said. “The championship programme was developed with a television audience at its heart, allowing for more storytelling around the athletes, while also engaging fans more effectively through digital platforms.” It sounds like it will have the curated reality of an episode of Alone.

Advertisement

The infield is black to literally block out distracting action when events are not on and athletes are not competing, meaning each event is spotlighted. Not just that: “A bespoke sound identity will reflect the vibe and energy of the Ultimate brand, with pole vault world record-holder Mondo Duplantis in charge of delivering the Ultimate Anthem.” If you have any idea what that word salad means you might win a medal. Well, you might … if The Ultimate issued them. The athletes at this event will not compete for medals, they’ll vie for a share of the $US10 million in prizemoney – each winner will get $150k and a quirky, as yet unrevealed, trophy. For the record, the Ultimate Anthem is the song Duplantis wrote and sang for the event. You read that right.

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

NFL 2026 Singing, cheering and an American takeover: Why the NFL’s MCG experiment was a smash hit This is part of the unashamed attempt to engage and use the biggest names in the sport to decide what the event should look like how to make the sport better. It is arguably a smarter approach than asking only marketeers, broadcasters or influencers. So Usain Bolt, still the biggest figure in the sport, years after retiring as the greatest athlete ever, is helping curate the event. Noah Lyles, the current sprint champion and showman, has been consulting on how to crank the in-stadium, on-TV, hype and excitement. Sadly, consulting will be as close as he gets because he injured himself last month and had to pull out of competition. Tennis-style on-court interviews are being held with athletes in the stadium. The push, post the success of TV’s Drive to Survive, is to leverage the personality of the athletes, not the athletics, to engage new audiences. So all athletes will immediately be given access to footage and photos of themselves competing to push on their digital channels and social media. It will create a circular marketing tool for sport and athlete. The danger some sports have found showcasing the “real person” is discovering the athlete is as interesting as hydronic heating.

Advertisement

Fortunately, athletics has some with spunk, hence, despite not automatically qualifying, Jakob Ingebrigtsen and Josh Kerr will both race the mile. Really, they couldn’t not be there. They are the hottest head-to-head race in the world right now. Norwegian Jakob Ingebrigsten is one of the stars on show at the Ultimate Championships. AP Photo/Beata Zawrzel Ingebrigtsen, the Norwegian punk with a boy-band hairstyle, tatts and good looks, is not only imperiously quick and one of the best the world has ever seen, he is also one of the most cavalier and indiscreet interviewees in sport. It is not just Scandinavian bluntness, he simply could not give fewer f---s. Like Lyles, Sha Carri Richardson and Mondo Du Plantis, Ingebrigtsen is box office. He had to be there. The reigning Olympic champions are all automatically invited, as are the reigning world champions and the Diamond League winners and the organisers retain discretion in the invitation-only event to make sure the athletes people actually want to see are featured.

Related Article Updated

Australian cricket ‘Dire consequences’: BBL sell-off slammed amid fears for grassroots cricket In Australia we have seen this sort of concept before with Nitro. Remember that? Well, this is a kind of Nitro Two. Ultimate Nitro? It looks like it could be a bit like Nitro … only better and sustainable. The NRL has backed two crucial officiating decisions that went against South Sydney in their 20-10 loss to Newcastle that prompted Rabbitohs coach Wayne Bennett to call for the bunker to be abolished. Bennett blasted the NRL bunker after a knock-on ruling against Alex Johnston denied the Rabbitohs a try at a vital stage during their elimination final defeat, declaring: “The quicker they get rid of the bunker, the happier I’ll be.” Loading There was also conjecture about the bunker’s decision to green-light a Knights try 10 minutes later when winger Dominic Young was deemed not to have put a foot on the sideline despite several angles suggesting his boot had touched the chalk. However, head office was comfortable with both calls after a thorough post-game review, according to sources who are aware of the verdict but not authorised to comment.

Advertisement

The tough calls aside, South Sydney were struggling when they lost Cody Walker to a calf injury just before half-time. They then lost to an impressive Knights side, who march on to week two of the finals for a showdown against the loser of Saturday afternoon’s Warriors-Dolphins clash. Approaching the hour mark at Allianz Stadium on Friday night, Latrell Mitchell squeezed a pass for Johnston who appeared to have the ball stripped from him by Knights back-rower Jermaine McEwen. Did Jeremaine McEwen strip the ball from Alex Johnston? Nine Play was allowed to continue and Johnston kneed the ball forward, then Jayden Sullivan kicked it further ahead before scoring. Referee Ashley Klein awarded a try, but bunker official Chris Butler had other ideas, claiming McEwen had been trying to make a tackle and that Johnston had lost the ball.

Advertisement

Instead of levelling the scores at 10-10 with a kick to come, Souths were put on the back foot – and 10 minutes later conceded a try to Young, who appeared to put his right foot on the touchline. The bunker is only required to uphold an on-field decision if there is inconclusive or insufficient evidence for it to make its own clear, independent determination. It means that the off-field official shouldn’t default to the referee’s original call, regardless of how fine the margin is. Which is why both contentious rulings ultimately went in the Knights’ favour. Loading Bennett complimented Newcastle on playing a “tremendous game”, and was mindful to not deflect from the result, but he was also frustrated with the bunker, which was established to eliminate contentious calls. “Anyone who plays rugby league or knows rugby league knows that was a knock-on,” Bennett said. “The ball was knocked out of his [Johnston’s] hands. The referee awards a try, then the bunker buys in and says it’s no try.

Advertisement

Cody Walker hobbles off with a calf injury. NRL “Ten minutes later, Newcastle winger Dom Young goes down the sideline, I’m not sure if he put his foot on the sideline, but the bottom line is the bunker comes back and says, ‘We’re going with the referee’s call’. “I want to know who is refereeing the game, that’s the first thing I want to know. Is it the bunker or is it the referee? “In the case of Alex Johnston ... you can look at that 50 times, everyone can come up with a different opinion. It’s just too technical. It’s not what the game needs. “I’ve been in the game a long time, I’ve seen a lot of things, and I don’t think the bunker enhances our game to the [level] we believe it does.”

Advertisement

Bennett said he was happy to live with referees making poor calls, just as he was prepared to cope with mistakes made by his players. “But the bunker was meant to be 100 per cent bulletproof, and it’s not,” he said. “It won’t stop here tonight. There will be more instances through the play-offs, I can promise you.” Bennett was also confused by a call in the first half to penalise Mitchell when he appeared to be struck first in an altercation with Knights centre Dane Gagai. The duel between Mitchell and Gagai was one of the highlights of the evening.

Advertisement

Newcastle coach Justin Holbrook thought “common sense prevailed” with the decision to strip Souths of the Sullivan try, while Cameron Smith said during the live commentary it did not deserve to be a try. The Knights looked like a team that was fresh from the bye the previous week, and looked in more sync in attack. Loading Souths were not helped by Walker breaking down on the half hour, with the playmaker immediately signalling to the sideline for help. He would have been unlikely to play on next weekend had Souths progressed, but Bennett confirmed the club was keen for him to play on in 2027, even though a deal was yet to be formally struck.

An early guilty plea will result in a $1800 fine, while he’ll pay $2,500 if he unsuccessfully contests it. Aside from Walker, then Johnston failing to finish the game with a groin complaint, Souths had enjoyed a good run with injuries at this time of year. title: ‘I wasn’t going to let him push me around’: Gagai opens up on Mitchell stoush
text:

Newcastle veteran Dane Gagai has spoken about his personal battle against Latrell Mitchell that lit up the opening night of the finals, declaring “I wasn’t going to let him push me around.” The Knights produced a monumental upset on Friday night, beating South Sydney 20-10 at Allianz Stadium despite the absence of Jacob Saifiti, Dylan Lucas, Dylan Brown and Trey Mooney. Loading One of the highlights of the match was the running battle between Gagai and Mitchell, who last week produced the tackle of the year on Roosters playmaker Toby Rodwell at the same ground. The former Rabbitohs teammates reprised a rivalry that had stretched for over a decade at club and State of Origin level that at one point threatened to spill over on Friday night. However, Gagai was confident it would never lead to punches or a player being sent to the sin bin.

Advertisement

“Nah, it was just a heat of the moment thing,” Gagai said. “And he’s obviously sticking up for his teammate. I was trying to get the ball off Alex Johnston, and he came over, stood up for his teammate. “I wasn’t going to let him push me around. And that’s the beauty of our game. When you get competitors like that on the field – and like I said, we know what Latrell brings to a team, and he’s those players you love playing alongside – so I just needed to be that player for our team. Latrell Mitchell and Dane Gagai. Nine “And yeah, we gave each other a big hug after the game and I love the big fella, especially the things he’s doing outside of footy and in the community. But on the field, we compete.” Gagai, who will join Brisbane next year, said he didn’t go out intending to target Mitchell.

Advertisement

“I don’t think it was an individual battle within myself personally,” he said. “I was just more thinking about what can I do to help the team out. And obviously, Latrell is a big part of their team … He’s a big-game player, and he’s a superstar of the game. “But I just had to focus on my preparation throughout the week, get myself right to put myself in a position to do my job for the team, whether that’s in defence or attack. Latrell Mitchell and Dane Gagai come to blows. Getty Images “I’m always going to compete and I always look forward to the opportunity of coming up against players like that. They obviously always bring the best out of you because if you have a little micro slip, then they can punish you pretty quick. I’m just grateful that we come away with the win.” Gagai has maintained an incredible level of performance during his 16-year NRL career. The 35-year-old said he took no heed from some critics’ calls for him to end it.

“I don’t really listen to what other people say, and I kind of know within myself my abilities and what I’m capable of,” he said. “I guess I won’t let anyone retire me when I’m not ready. I still feel like I’m playing good footy. The body feels good. I still love the game, I still love competing. And like I said before, once I lose either the passion to play the game or the body can’t perform and keep up, then until then, I’m going to keep playing this beautiful game of rugby league and keep trying to win.” ‘He’s getting better every week’: Resurgent Rabbitoh on Walters’ World Cup radar David Fifita’s resurgence for South Sydney has earned him a place in Australia’s extended World Cup squad, while teammate Latrell Mitchell is also making a late bid for a Kangaroos jersey after sending a goalkicking SOS to a Canberra legend. An emotional Fifita this week spoke about overcoming “dark days” when injuries left him wondering if he would ever recapture his devastating early-career form.
