Loading Friday’s elimination final against the Newcastle Knights was a day before the one-year anniversary of his father’s death. Fifita’s barnstorming runs on the right edge, especially over the past month, have not escaped the attention of Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters, whose starting back-rowers from last year’s Ashes, Hudson Young and Angus Crichton, are injured and linking with rugby respectively. Penrith’s Liam Martin, Canterbury’s Jacob Preston, North Queensland’s Reuben Cotter, Fifita and Souths teammate Tallis Duncan have all been included in the preliminary 40-man squad all World Cup nations had to submit last Friday. Players can be added from outside the squad at a later date. David Fifita’s form has caught the attention of Kangaroos’ coach Kevin Walters. James Brickwood/SMH

“David is an elite player, and he’s put himself in the frame by getting back to the form we all know he’s capable of,” Walters said on Thursday. “He’s a big man, he likes to use his weight and power to his advantage – he loves the physical stuff. Because he’s such a big body, he needs to play regularly, which he’s been doing. He’s getting better each week, and the further Souths progress into the finals will only help him.” Souths captain Cameron Murray will be back in the green and gold should he remain fit, especially with question marks over the fitness of Panthers lock Isaah Yeo, while Mitchell is also in the frame for the end-of-season World Cup. “A person of Latrell’s calibre, the more footy he can play at this time of year, the more he’ll push his chances – we saw last week what he can do and what he brings to a team,” Walters said of Mitchell. Canberra legend Jarrod Croker spent Tuesday helping Latrell Mitchell with his goalkicking. South Sydney Rabbitohs

Advertisement

Fifita played for the Prime Minister’s XIII and Australia’s nines team in 2019, but his only Test appearances were for Tonga at the 2022 World Cup. Meanwhile, Raiders sharpshooter Jarrod Croker made the hit-and-run trip to Heffron Park on Tuesday to work with fellow left-footed kicker Mitchell. Souths’ goalkicking strike rate of 64.7 per cent (88 from 136) this season is the worst in the NRL. Improved kicking could have been the difference between fifth and sixth when you consider Cronulla finished level on competition points but 36 ahead on differential – equivalent to 18 goals. Related Article NRL 2026 The Roosters called out Latrell over the ‘hit of the year’. On Tuesday, he returned serve Mitchell himself has kicked 41 of 65 attempts for a strike rate of 63.1 per cent. He slotted 61 from 78 (78.2 per cent) in 2022.

Advertisement

Croker, who lives on the Gold Coast, launched his own range of kicking tees, known as “284”, a nod to his Canberra Raiders playing number. The tees are used by Mitchell. “He reached out on the Monday, and I was at training on Tuesday,” Croker said. “The other night [against the Roosters] was his first full game back from injury, so there was a bit of fatigue, and he didn’t really have much of an exit. “An ‘exit’ is like your follow through, which gets harder when you get wider out, and only because kickers want to kick the ball harder, then stop and look up to see where it’s going. “I told him to try and keep the follow through happening, and aim it just inside the left post. The key is, ‘Aim small, miss small’, and if he’s aiming just inside that left post with his natural shape, he’ll be thereabouts most of the time.” ‘Money’s not everything’: The contract conundrum facing Panthers

Adrian Proszenko Penrith enforcers Moses Leota and Liam Martin have spoken of the agonising decisions they will soon be required to make on their playing careers, with the latter declaring “money’s not everything at the end of the day”. The Panthers have a raft of key stars uncontracted beyond 2027 who will be free to negotiate with rival clubs on November 1. Some of them – headlined by Nathan Cleary, Isaah Yeo, Martin, Leota and Isaiah Papali’i – have parked negotiations to focus on the upcoming finals, beginning with Sunday’s blockbuster clash against the Roosters at CommBank Stadium. Loading The club has made progress with Yeo, who was able to dedicate some time to his contract discussions while recovering from a pectoral injury, while Cleary is in no rush to make a call.

Advertisement

The club granted Leota a brief window to explore his options earlier this season, but the Kiwi international hasn’t made a decision on where he will be playing in 2028. Martin, who has been strongly linked with the PNG Chiefs, will also be in hot demand if he doesn’t recommit to Penrith before November 1. The NSW and Australian back-rower said he would “love to stay” at the Panthers, but would give his future more attention after their premiership campaign ends. “Obviously there could be more money elsewhere, but money’s not everything at the end of the day,” Martin said. “It’s also enjoying your footy. I’ve got a great bunch of mates here, like best mates, that I’ve played with since I was 18. Liam Martin has a big call to make on his future. Getty Images “And I’ve been in Penrith for 10 years now, and got a little boy. So, yeah, there’s a lot to weigh up. It’s not an easy decision, but I guess I’ll have to make it in due time.”

Advertisement

Martin and Leota have been the cornerstones of a Panthers pack that has won four premierships since 2021. They will have to balance the prospect of higher wages available elsewhere against the likelihood of joining a less successful team. “That success is so addictive, and what we’ve got here is just an incredible culture,” Martin said. “And it’s going to be very successful for a long time, this club, when you have the likes of Casey [McLean], Blaze [Talagi], Billy Phillips coming through. So, yeah, it would be hard to walk away … Related Article NRL 2026 ‘How is he doing this?’: Panthers teammates awed by skipper Yeo’s return from ruptured pec “It’s sort of the duality of it. You couldn’t imagine going somewhere and experiencing failure and just how tough that would be. But also the challenge of building a successful club somewhere else, and I feel like I could offer something. It’s a tough decision.” Leota is grappling with similar sentiments before making a call on what will likely be the last contract of his career.

title: Everyday items linked to autism risk
text:
Exposure to chemicals found in everyday plastics during pregnancy may increase the likelihood of children developing autistic and ADHD traits, research has claimed.

A lengthy study conducted at Florey Institution of Neuroscience and Mental Health claims to have established a link between the chemical DEHP and neurodivergent conditions.

DEHP is found in several everyday plastic items, such as food container lids.

Started in 2010, the study focused on 800 Australian families, tracking them from the mother's pregnancy through to the formative years of the children.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Through urine samples taken at late-term pregnancy, researchers were able to ascertain the DEHP exposure levels of the mothers while carrying their children.

And through a series of check-ins throughout their development, they were then able to track which children had developed symptoms of autism and ADHD.

The research then found that the children whose mothers had greater levels of exposure during pregnancy had developed the most traits – establishing what researchers believe to be a link.

And the study's latest report not only establishes the link, but claims to be able to explain why this happens.

The study may explain the link between exposure and neurodivergent traits. Picture: iStock

"Our study found infants exposed to higher levels of DEHP before birth showed distinctive changes in DNA methylation – an epigenetic switch that turns genes on and off – in their umbilical cord blood at birth," lead author Sam Tanner said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"What we have found is a possible biological explanation."

The study found that exposure to the chemical likely triggered this "switch", making the gene that produces neurodivergent traits active, resulting in the child developing symptoms.

Prof Anne-Louise Ponsonby, who authored the report. Picture: Florey

Prof Anne-Louise Ponsonby, another of the study's authors, said its goal was to better understand the impact chemicals found in plastic have on people – which can then inform decision-makers on what regulations are needed.

"Almost all women in this Australian study showed exposure to the common DEHP chemical," she said.

"Chemical exposure levels are mainly determined at the population level and are not easily a matter of choice.

Advertisement Advertisement

"Plastic chemicals like DEHP are often ingested, so government safety regulations around food processing and packaging are very important."

DEHP is also found in some shower curtains.

What is DEHP?

DEHP. or Di- (2-Ethylhexyl) phthalate to give it its full scientific name, is a manufactured chemical which is used to make plastic products more flexible.

It is found in several commonly used household products, including things like food containers, cling wrap and food processing equipment.

It is also often found in shower curtains, non-slip bath mats and some types of vinyl flooring.

Prof Ponsonby said that generally, it finds its way into our bodies through no real fault of our own, with it not always being clear how and when exposure has happened.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has already taken some measures to limit exposure to the chemical – banning toys that contain more than one per cent DEHP.

But researchers are calling for further measures to limit people being exposed to it.

"Global plastic control efforts should take into consideration the recent evidence as it emerges on the need for health protection, particularly for vulnerable populations such as pregnant woman and young babies," Prof Ponsonby said.
